title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Cabal of Chaos (Updated October 13, 2026)
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific Detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Cabal of Chaos Detachment for Chaos Space Marines.

Introduced initially in mid 2025 as part of a quarterly balance update and updated with the initial deluge of 11th edition Detachments, the Cabal of Chaos focuses primarily on the faction's psykers and Daemon Prince units, buffing them in interesting ways and giving you added buffs when playing them.

Changelog

  • 10-13-2026 (Current): Updated for 11th edition and the September Balance Update
  • 6-4-2025: Initial Publication
Disposition: Disruption

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

The Cabal of Chaos Detachment gives Chaos Space Marines a new way to build armies around PSYKER and DAEMON PRINCE units, giving units additional bonuses when they make a Dark Pact near one of those units. This can either be additional strength on their ranged attacks near Psykers or Extra AP on melee attacks near a Daemon Prince. Additionally, there are some solid Stratagems and Enhancements here to buff units and reward you for taking Psykers in your army.

Although initially not much of a factor in 11th edition, as CSM armies have moved toward taking 2 DP Detachments, the Cabal of Chaos has seen more play, primarily because it's the only 1 DP Detachment offering much of value without forcing you to take units you might not want to take and the new update

Detachment Rule: Empyric Wellspring

There are two parts to this:

  • In your Shooting phase, when a friendly HERETIC ASTARTES PSYKER unit (excluding DAEMON units) is selected to shoot, if that unit makes a Dark Pact, its ranged attacks have +1 S.
  • In the Fight phase, when a friendly HERETIC ASTARTES DAEMON PRINCE unit (excluding KHORNE units)  is selected to fight, if that unit makes a Dark Pact, it gets +2 S and +1 AP on its melee attacks.

This is a pretty limited rule, and shooting buffs on psyker units are kind of limited in their utility, though we'll look at where they provide the most value. At a quick glance, your non-Daemon Psyker Units in the Chaos Space Marines army are:

  • Sorcerer
  • Sorcerer in Terminator Armour
  • Dark Commune
  • Masters of the Maelstrom
  • Master of Possession
  • Nemesis Claw

At first glance, that's not a great selection of units to give +1 Strength on their Shooting attacks. That said, the recent September 2026 balance update pushing combi-weapons and combi-bolters to S5 AP-1 suddenly makes +1 Strength a lot more interesting, as it means firing at S6 with combi-bolters and combi-weapons when you pact, and that means you can effectively punch up into a lot more targets. There's a very real play now in taking units of 10 terminators with a Terminator Sorcerer in Warpstrike Champions, where your units can go back into deep strike and get built-in re-rolls to Advance and Charge rolls from the Sorcerer, plus you can use Death Hex for Extra AP. A unit of ten Terminators dropping S6 Bolter shots at AP-2 with Lethal or Sustained Hits and full re-rolls to hit is a real threat - just ask any Thousand Sons player.

The Nemesis Claw are also interesting here as they come with the PSYKER keyword natively and so just have built-in +1S on their shooting attacks when making a Dark Pact. Their shooting isn't particularly great, but you can give them a Heavy Bolter if you take ten models, and having a S10 meltagun shot is pretty funny. Legionaries can also be interesting now with a bunch of S5 AP-1 bolters, but generally speaking these are both melee units, so the benefit is ore like a fun add-on than something you'd actually build around.

The other big option here is Daemon Princes, where getting +2S and +1AP in melee helps make the Winged Daemon Prince legitimately interesting as a threat, sending his hellforged weapons to S10 AP-3 on the strike and S8 AP-1 on the sweep. That +2 Strength gets you over some solid breakpoints and ensures you're still wounding basic marines on a 2+, and the extra AP is basically necessary to ensure you're not whiffing against key targets. Add in Death Hex from a Terminator Sorcerer and your Daemon Prince can actually put in work.

Terminator Sorcerer. Credits: That Gobbo

Enhancements

These enhancements are fine. There's not a ton to take them over other options. Touched by the Warp is more cute than useful, though Conduit is great on a Daemon Prince.

  • Touched by the Warp (10 points) - Heretic Astartes model only, can’t go on a Khorne model. The model has PSYKER and its weapons have [PSYCHIC]. Because this only applies to one model, it’s tough to make it work. The problem here is that you just don’t really have characters who are good enough at shooting to make this viable. The only one which comes to mind is the Lord Discordant, who can carry an autocannon and might want to avoid catching modifiers to hit. The other place you’d theoretically use this is on a Warpsmith joining Havocs to give them the PSYKER keyword but they already ignore modifiers to hit so you’re at best just trying to get them +1 Strength, which can be helpful on Autocannons. The actual value of this is more in the ability to trigger some of the Stratagems here, like Infernal Vigour and Wreathed in Warpflame.
  • Conduit of Chaos (20 points) - Daemon model only (excluding KHORNE models). The model’s melee attacks have [LANCE]. Oh hell yeah. This one is huge when you pair it with the +2 Strength from the Dark Pact. S10 and Lance will wound most things on a 2+ and can punch up effectively into tougher threats on a 4+, helping shore up one of the big problems with the Daemon Prince’s melee.

Stratagems

The Stratagems here are solid. They’re all priced at 1 CP, meaning you won’t have many issues around CP generation. Your bigger challenge will be wanting to use all of them all the time.

  • Infernal Vigour (1 CP) - Used in your Command phase on a friendly PSYKER or DAEMON unit (not KHORNE). That unit heals D3+1 wounds. This is really great for Terminators, as it means more often than not you can get back a full 3-wound model when you throw this out. It's also great on Chosen or Possessed if you're going that route, but regenerating Terminators for your big units is the real value.
  • Fleshy Curse (1 CP) - Used at the start of your Shooting phase. Pick a Psyker unit and a visible enemy unit within 12” of them. Roll a D6. On a 1 they take 1 mortal wound. On a 24 they take D3, and on a 5-6 they take 2D3 mortal wounds. This is all done by a psychic attack. This is great - it’s a solid grenade-like substitute, and can combine with a grenade just as easily for extra mortal wounds.
  • Wreathed in Warpflame (1 CP) - Used in your Shooting phase, when a PSYKER unit is picked to shoot. That unit’s attacks gain [IGNORES COVER]. Given that Psychic attacks already ignore modifiers to hit, this is purely a benefit for the non-psyker models in the unit. Which means it's great on your Terminators when you need to push through extra hits against a horde unit. Don't bother with it if you're going into something that requires [LETHAL HITS] for punching up, though - just let the full re-rolls do the work as you fish for lethals.
Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

Playing This Detachment

We didn't think much of this Detachment when it originally released, and that's partly because at the time, it focused on units you just weren't taking in your CSM lists. However the Cabal of Chaos slowly became a more common pick for CSM armies, primarily because it was often  the only 1 DP Detachment offering anything of value to your army and because it was an easy way to get the Disruption disposition in teams environments. With the release of the new September Balance update, things have shifted dramatically.

Essentially, giving Chaos Terminators S5 AP-1 bolters changes the entire calculus on their utility. The Thousand Sons built an entire strategy around having AP-2 bolters with re-rolls to hit and Lethal hits firing en masse at major threats and now CSM armies can just do the same by pairing a Terminator Sorcerer (and Death Hex) with a unit of Terminators, who gain full re-rolls to hit whenever they make a Dark Pact. The result is a deluge of S5 AP-2 shooting with either LETHAL or SUSTAINED HITS 1 and full re-rolls to hit firing into a target. The obvious pairing here becomes the Warpstrike Champions Detachment, which lets said Terminator unit go back up into Deep Strike each round, then drop in to repeat the process, staying out of trouble. Because volume is key here and hitting on a 4+ before modifiers sucks, you'll want to kit your terminators out now with Combi-bolters and not combi-weapons. Losing the dev wounds isn't amazing, but you'll make up for it with the extra volume.

If you don't want to go the terminator route, you have some other options. Cabal pairs nicely with Chaos Cult, which has its own built-in psykers (and loves being able to grenade targets with Fleshy Curse), and benefits from adding in lone Terminator Sorcerers and Winged Daemon Princes. If you're going heavy on regular marine bodies, then pairing this Detachment with something like Veterans of the Long War can work as well - a unit of Chosen with Masters of the Maelstrom and Fabius Bile can be really nasty, and will makes for an amazing target when it comes to healing via the Infernal Vigour Stratagem (especially because you can double heal with Garreon reviving one model and the Stratagem giving you another, or use your free CP to immediately heal).

Strengths

  • Terminator Sorcerers. Hands-down the best PSYKER option in the army, Terminator Sorcerers now give your units a ton of value, and make 20 terminator strategies viable. Being able to heal them via Stratagem or give your unit [IGNORES COVER] is also huge, and add a lot to the mix.
  • Daemon Princes. Chaos Daemon Princes can be a bit underwhelming at times but here the extra AP really helps them push through the one extra wound they need to be respectable. The walking Daemon Princes’ upgrade to gain a conditional Lone Operative ability synergizes well with their role to hang out and buff units, and the flying Daemon Princes hit quite hard here.

Weaknesses

  • Narrow benefits. Outside of Terminator Sorcerers and Daemon Princes, the buffs here just aren't that useful. +1 Strength on ranged attacks is only good on specific units, and it really only started mattering to Terminators when they got +1 AP on their bolters.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

A Sample List

The key thing here we're building around is 20 terminators, paired with Sorcerers in Terminator Armour. They go up, they come down, and they light up a target with insane amounts of AP-2 bolter shooting before doing the whole thing again. The big downside? You're stuck playing Disruption.

This is nasty - your three big hammer units are the Terminator bricks and Kravek + Mutilators, and you can pickup two each per turn. One of them gets a turn 1 Deep strike while the other gets beefier shooting, and as an added bonus you have a nasty flying threat in the form of the Winged Daemon Prince. Your biggest challenges here are going to be finding the CP to do everything you want and the fact that you are stuck playing Disruption - in particular your matchup into Purge is a nightmare. So just focus on tabling your opponent and using the Bikers/Raiders/Cultists to do your actions as needed and using the big bricks of terminators to eliminate key threats.

I'll readily admit this list has more legs in teams than singles right now, but the core threat of two big terminator bricks ready to throw down at T6 and spitting out insane amounts of AP-2 firepower is very solid. You're basically pulling the same trick Scarabs did, only at a discount, and with more reliable access to full re-rolls to hit.

Final Thoughts

What a glow-up. The change to bolters has had a dramatic impact on this Detachment's utility, turning it from a nothingburger you take as your 1 DP filler into something you can legitimately build around in Warpstrike Champions. There are a number of interesting ways to build around this Detachment now, and it figures to be a very competitive option moving forward.

title: The Paint Review: Monument Hobbies ProAcryl 1Step Phase Two
content:
Greetings, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to another paint review. We bring you a double act this time - I, keewa, your pundit of pigment, am joined by the formidable Contemptor Kevin to discuss the second wave of the ProAcryl 1Step range from Monument Hobbies.

We’ve already discussed the general idea of 1Step in the first review, which you can find here, but I offer you a short recap or précis here: 1Step is the long-awaited entry of Monument Hobbies into the area of the market generally called “Contrast-style” paints, characterised by their fluidity and staining - paints like Army Painter Speedpaints, Vallejo Xpress Color, and so on and so on. Every man and his dog seems to have a trademark-friendly range of contrast-style paints these days, and so Monument’s very late entry into the arena raised a few eyebrows, but plenty of excitement as well.

With thanks to Monument Hobbies for providing keewa with a copy of 1Step Wave 2 for review. Contemptor Kevin purchased his copy of the paints himself. 

Scarlet Red

Keewa: The first wave of 1Step paints was lacking a “proper red”. Crimson (a lovely colour) technically counts as a red, certainly, but that’s already dark and quite desaturated - Scarlet Red is much beefier and has a lot more punch in the saturation department. It’s very impactful, though it’ll take a few coats to cover fully; bear that in mind when it goes on pink over white at first.

Contemptor Kevin: My big test with it was to slap it on a pre-highlighted/shadowed red cloak, the one I used for my Victrix Guard Ancient.  One use and I was absolutely sold on this paint.  

Rust

Keewa: Previously a colour only available to attendees of Adepticon; now in Wave 2, Rust is available to everyone. The first 1-Step set featured a very saturated reddish “hot” Orange; now the range includes Rust as a darker and more natural oxide orange with a brownish tint. As you might guess from the name of the colour, an oxide orange is the perfect colour for painting naturally weathered iron and steel, and the high flow of 1Step allows the painter to create easy streaking rust stains. Grimdark and Blanche-esque painters will like this one.

Bronze Yellow

Keewa: A similar relationship to Warm Yellow as Rust is to Orange, Bronze Yellow is a dark, warm, earthy ochre yellow with a brownish tint. It’s ideal for shading “standard” yellows into a more natural register, as well as fur and hair. 

Contemptor Kevin: I wish I had a pot of Nazdreg Yellow to compare this to Bronze Yellow, because both *I think* are similar paints.  This one might be the weakest link in the set, because it occupies a niche between Olive Yellow and Warm Yellow.  I'm happy to have it and it's a good paint to use, but it's much more subtle versus some of the other paints.  

Olive Yellow

Keewa: I think the best way to describe Olive Yellow is to call it a “dirty” yellow. It’s not necessarily super desaturated, but it has a good amount of both brown and green. It’ll probably find plenty of use shading things like Cadian khaki fatigues, stone textures, and general grime application.

Contemptor Kevin: I think Keewa hits the nail on the head.  For those looking at Contrast comparisons, it's more of an easier-to-use/more pigment-dense Plaguebearer Flesh.  My use of it suggests that it could make a great shade color for Plaguebearer Flesh for some extremely quick but nice-looking NMM-aged gold.  Here. I used the Olive Yellow to shade the PBF.

Yellow Green

Keewa: My very first thought upon seeing this paint was “Ork skin in a bottle”; this paint has everything I want from an Ork skin - the colour is punchy with a lot of depth and versatility. Since it’s transparent, you can change how it behaves by underpainting with different colours, adjusting the warmth and coolness of the highlights and shadows to achieve everything from a bright yellow-y goblinoid skin to one with bluish shadows.  Yellow Green also excels as both a colour of nature and decay, ideal for your wood-elves, moss and leaves on Sylvaneth tree-people, ooze on Death Guard and Nurgle daemons, etc.  

Contemptor Kevin: For the most part, I have been using Contrast Warp Lightning as a filter to give my Orks a very punchy skin tone.  I don't think that will change for me, because there's a bunch of underlayers that Warp Lightning filters.  But directly over a very light primer?  I think Yellow Green looks better:

Dark Turquoise

Keewa: Oh boy, oh boy, everyone knows that I love turquoise, and this one is a real beauty, sailing right up the list of Paints I Love. First things first, a quibbling nitpick: this paint is not dark, and I do not understand why it is labelled as such. The unusually unhelpful naming mirrors Dark Turquoise from the normal ProAcryl line, which is also not dark - what ProAcryl calls Dark Turquoise I would just call Turquoise. That’s by the by, though; this paint has punch in spades, a beautifully vibrant and intense colour. This paint is ideal for plasma coils + power glow, lizardmen scales, and magic spells.

Contemptor Kevin:  I suspect the reason why this is called Dark Turquoise is also to let us know that this isn't just the 1-Step version of Contrast Akhelian Green, but that this paint is much richer and has a lot more pigmentation than the venerable Warhammer paint.  Making a good looking Alpha Legion army with a metal undercoat and this paint has never been easier.  

Dark Green Blue

Keewa: In contrast to Dark Turquoise, Dark Green Blue actually is a dark turquoise colour with a strong oceanic, abyssal vibe. It’s obviously darker, but the saturation is dialled down, and the result is a paint that is greener, but also considerably colder. If Dark Turquoise is the colour of the sea at a Caribbean beach, Dark Green Blue is the colour of the raging South Atlantic. This paint is obviously an exceptional shade for both greens and blues, and also functions nicely as a good chromatic black for other applications where you need a black that’s freezing cold. 

Deep Blue

Keewa: Not the computer that gave Garry Kasparov a good shoeing. Deep Blue is more of an ultramarine than the regular phthalo–esque Blue of the first wave, with a bit more purple to it. This particular blue has a good deal of similarity to the regular ProAcryl Ultramarine in both tone and boldness. 

Contemptor Kevin: Ironically, this particular Blue is probably the best contrast-style paint for painting Ultramarines with a Warhammer Paint Macragge Blue tone.  The Contrast Ultramarines Blue is far too dark and desaturated.  This color has the same feel as Macragge Blue while remaining more vibrant than the Warhammer paint.  It won't replace how I do my blindingly blue Ultras, but for those who prefer the modern style (or want a darker color for Heresy), these will do the trick.

Black

Contemptor Kevin:  In Set #1, our darkest color was Dark Blue Black.  I noted at the time that it was a very dark blue and would work well for Ravenwing models, but it was very clearly not a true black.  Set #2 finally gives us the line’s true black, simply called “Black”.  Now, for the way I paint, Warhammer Paint Black Templar is one of my workhorse paints.  When I want to “reset” something to hide the color underneath it, such as when painting trim or details, it tends to get a coat of Black Templar. Testing these paints out on my Land Speeder, one coat of Black struggled to hide the base color.  It worked fine with blues, but over a gold it changed the color to dark gold.  Another caveat I had with it is that it tends to dry a fair bit slower than Black Templar: This means using it to try and paint the rim of the base black was more fraught than I thought it was going to be.  Sadly, I don't think this 1Step is going to replace my beloved Black Templar on the brush.  

Keewa: I disagree with my learned colleague; I find that the slow drying time of the 1Step paints makes them ideal for glazing shadows. If I compare this to Army Painter Speedpaint Grim Black, I really appreciate the slower drying time; with the AP paint, you have hardly any time on your hands before it begins to form a skin and tears with a bit of manipulation. This paint will be ideal for blacklining and separation; I think it’s going to become a favourite for me and many others.

Bright Slate Grey

Keewa: Going to start calling this one Notpothecary White. ProAcryl has a reputation for excellent whites, and although this isn’t called a white, it’s no exception, and there’s no doubt what it’s for. It’s a very similar tone to the venerable Apothecary White, but it’s better. Why? The extended drying time of the 1Step formula means that it’s a lot easier to move the paint off the flat areas where you don’t want it, deftly helping to avoid the telltale coffee stains and tide marks that plague contrast painting. If you’re painting white, you really need this.

Contemptor Kevin: Keewa is underselling this one.  This paint is better than Apothecary White (and the second attempt, Soulblight Grey) in every way.  The flow is far superior, and the bottle design (with a built-in mixer) makes actually using this paint substantially easier.  Vis-à-vis Soulblight Grey, this produced a cooler white, but a smoother and nicer white.  

Dark Brown

From the top clockwise: Dark Brown, Warhammer Paint Cygor Brown, Warhammer Paint Snakebite Leather, Warm Brown, Warhammer Paint Wyldwood, Army Painter Speedpaint Satchel Brown.

Contemptor Kevin: As you can see, this brown is very different from the last set’s Warm Brown, being, if not necessarily darker, then containing much less red and feeling much more desaturated.  This color strikes me as an obvious choice for older wood or even a muddy texture.  One interesting property I found with this paint is that it went over the GW White Scar-primed base pretty easily.  By contrast, the Warhammer Paint Contrasts were pretty quick to pull away from the surface and bead up.  Accordingly, I was able to get an even coat of Dark Brown easily, but the other browns proved more challenging.  

Keewa: Compared to Warm Brown, Dark Brown strays into a colder, more Van Dyke Brown territory, and as such, it’s a pretty good shadow colour for Warm Brown.

Loading...

Dark Purple

Keewa: Compared to the Royal Purple that came with the first wave, Dark Purple occupies the other side of the purple spectrum - where Royal Purple skews towards the warmer Magenta side, Dark Purple is decidedly in the cold Indigo-Purple realm, on the cusp of being a dark blue. This colour contrast actually makes it an ideal shade for warmer purples like Royal Purple. 

Clockwise from Top: Dark Purple, Ultramarines Blue, Hive Dweller Purple, Cloudburst Blue, Royal Purple, Shyish Purple

Contemptor Kevin: Dark Purple sits in a position where it's not quite a purple, but not quite a blue.  It's also different from basically most of the other purples in the Contrast line.  I think Keewa is right - this is going to be a wonderful shadow color for Royal Purple, or as a bridge color for certain muzzle burns/heat warping for metal.  

Final Thoughts

Keewa: Rather than being another straightforward Contrast-Clone, Monument has sought to carve out a niche and establish 1Step as being a premium paint “along the same lines as Contrast, but different” - the lengthened drying time makes manipulating the paint on the model much easier. 1Step flows through the airbrush in the same manner as an ink, and unlike Army Painter Speedpaints, 1Step doesn’t foul up the needle by drying on the tip as it leaves the airbrush; honestly, with the way I tend to paint, using 1Step as airbrush filters is probably my biggest utility for these kinds of paints, so the drying time extender comes very much in handy. The Secret Sauce medium also works well as a thinner for both airbrushing and glazing. 

On the consumer side of things, at 6 euros per 22ml bottle, these paints can hardly be accused of being cheap. While not necessarily as ridiculously expensive as Contrast paint (more on that in a minute), 1Step considerably outstrips other contrast-a-likes (Xpress Color, Speedpaint etc.) both in bottle price and price per ml. Since ProAcryl positions itself as a “premium” brand, this is basically to be expected, but it’ll still sting your wallet – that’s 140-ish euros for the current range of 24 paints.

The 1Step paints are great; I find myself reaching for them all the time. They’re quite easy to recommend - even if the cost of buying in is a little steep.

Contemptor Kevin:  You get what you pay for in these paints, in my opinion.  These paints are all unique colors and extremely easy to use, both in terms of airbrushing and in terms of brush painting.  With the exception of the Black and potentially Bronze Yellow, these tones do not really overlap with Contrast, and thus having both is helpful. I'm not as keen on Black as Keewa is, but that's because I use Black Templar in a bit different manner than he does, where having the GW Pot design is a boon.  I like having sets of both, though I will readily agree that this stuff is better through the airbrush than Speedpaint.   Have any questions or feedback? title: "It shouldn't be fun, and it's not": What playing the world's longest board game is really like
content:
The Campaign for North Africa is an infamously arcane war board game, which takes longer to play than the WW2 campaign it depicts. Andy and James, a pair of friends from England, have completed the six turn tutorial, playing weekly for two entire years, and Stockholm syndrome is fast setting in.

I caught up with the pair, who document their efforts through the podcast 'War with a Mate', as they prepare to embark on the full campaign… of 50 turns. They say they fully expect this game to be a "permanent fixture" in their lives for decades, more set in stone than their jobs, their co-workers, and the places they live. James says, "20 years feels like a good estimate, and I can't think of anything I've kept consistent since I was ten."

Completing The Campaign for North Africa seems not only to be a test of endurance, grinding out turns, but also a battle of wits. Decoding the rulebook is a battle in itself. Written in 1978, it has painstakingly detailed rulings for everything up to and including the amount of water required to cook pasta, but also some frustrating vague patches.

"It mentions at one point in the rules… you can't air transport live camels, but you can transport, by air, dead camels," explains Andy.

"Now, there's only one unit that uses camels in the entire game - part of the Saharan detachment. But there's no way to determine if an individual camel is dead, and even more so how you would load that into an aircraft, or why you would load that into an aircraft. So it's just a small part of the rules in this vast sea of words that we spend ages trying to decipher, and we still don't really know what it means."

 

As they describe their adventures individually rolling one-on-one plane battles to simulate dogfights with 100+ aircraft, or being unable to press an attack because the truck with all their bullets broke down, one question is in the forefront of my mind.

And when I ask if they're actually enjoying themselves, Andy's answer is rather diplomatic. "The amount of work you have to put in to get the small nuggets of fun aren't quite congruent," he says.

He describes how the short flashes of action are broken up by tens of hours of admin and logistics preparation, and says that most of their time with the game is spent doing spreadsheets. "It shouldn't be fun, and it's not".

Andy and James often joke about having Stockholm syndrome for the Campaign for North Africa.

"We'll get to some of the combat sections of the game, and it feels like it's the most fun we've had in weeks," Andy says. "But in reality, if you were to put that in a vacuum, it's not a very exciting aspect of the game."

"I was complaining up until the last turn that I wasn't having fun", he adds, but says that in the hiatus, he finds there's a bit of a hole in his week.

James notes that the slow pace and the painstaking work required does make it satisfying when he can see the fruits of his labor.

"You might have a plan, and then you've spent a month getting all your trucks in the right place, and then it does feel good when those come off because you've been thinking about it for, like, a month," he says.

On the flipside, when those plans don't come together, it is devastating. Andy describes flicking through the rules at his desk or on the bus to double check he hasn't made an error and says that a turn where "one of the plans I had hinged on a rule that didn't quite exist" was the closest either of them came to quitting for good. "I do remember just walking away from the board and saying a few choice words to myself," he says.

James says if the "accountability tool" of the podcast hadn't kicked in, they both might have given up long ago. But what began as a way to keep the challenge going has wildly outperformed their expectations, getting close to around 30,000 listeners - they say, mostly from Australia.

Right now the duo is preparing for the long haul of the full campaign, and it seems while the two-year 'dry-run' has helped clear up plenty of rules confusions, there's still a lot of unfamiliar territory left to explore. James says, "The Commonwealth has this whole production system, but you have to plan it two months in advance, and because a turn is a week, our six turn practice didn't even get to that. So there's this whole branch of systems that I just haven't even touched yet, which is a bit daunting."

Meanwhile, the Axis, controlled by Andy, don't see the Germans join until about turn 27, so that's a lot of unfamiliar units to dig into.

I'll leave you with one detail I found delightful. In this ridiculous game which takes a decade or more to complete, the Axis gets a once-per-game torpedo strike ability. "I'll need to really pick my moment for that," Andy says. "It's once in the whole game, so that really has to count. If I use that and it doesn't pay off, I will be in tears."

Join the Wargamer Discord to hear more about this board game, and others that are probably more fun!

title: The 29 most expensive Yugioh cards in 2026
content:
What are the most expensive Yugioh cards? Since the card game launched in 1999, collectors of rare YuGiOh cards have paid millions of dollars to get their hands on historic, storied, and unique cards. This guide profiles the 29 most expensive Yugioh cards ever, with the highest price they've sold for - and we've verified them all.

Before we start talking money, here's another guide of hideously pricey cards to check out: the most expensive rare Pokémon cards. Or, if you want to stick to Yugioh, here's the latest Yugioh banlist update.

The most expensive Yugioh cards ever sold are:

  • Tyler the Great Warrior
  • Alt Art Gemini Elf T3 04
  • Masahiro the Dark Clown Tournament Prize
  • Blue Eyes White Dragon LOB 1st Edition
  • Crush Card Virus Shonen Jump Championship 2007
  • Minerva, the Exalted Lightsworn 2015 Prize Card
  • Cyber Dragon GX Toy Promo
  • Cyber Stein Shonen Jump Championship 2004
  • KC Grand Tournament 2nd Place Dark Magician
  • Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth Dark Duel Stories Promo
  • The Seal of Orichalcos UDE Event
  • Blue Eyes White Dragon Dark Duel Stories Promo
  • Chaos Emperor, the Dragon of Armageddon Prize Card
  • Dark Magician LOB 1st Edition
  • Card of Sanctity Kids WB Promo
  • Doomcaliber Knight Shonen Jump Championship 2008
  • Morphing Jar Tournament Pack 2 Promo
  • Corrected Art Dark Paladin 1st Edition
  • German Pharaoh's Tour Prize Gold Sarcophagus
  • Dark Magician Girl 1st Edition
  • TG Hyper Librarian
  • Red Eyes Black Dragon LOB 1st Edition
  • Number 89: Diablosis the Mind Hacker Championship 2017
  • Gaia the Dragon Champion 1st Edition
  • Blue Eyes Shining Dragon Retro Pack 2
  • Gladiator's Assault Magic Formula
  • Exodia Legend Of Blue Eyes White Dragon 1st Edition
  • Attack of the Giant Card Cyber Dragon
  • Stainless Steel Black Luster Soldier

Tyler the Great Warrior

Worth $311,211

The most expensive Yugioh card of all time is Tyler the Great Warrior, a one-of-a-kind card designed by a 14-year-old, which sold for over $300k.

The card, created by Tyler Gressle in 2005 as part of a Make-a-Wish request, is the rarest Yugioh card in existence - there is only one copy in the world. Gressle designed the card in 2005, when he was 14, and battling against a rare form of liver cancer.

18 years later, he decided to sell the card. The final auction bid racked up a whopping $311,211 (£249,793.51), meaning yes, this is officially the rarest and most expensive Yugioh card ever, period.

This valuable card is a wonderful memento of the Make-a-Wish Foundation's work, as well as Tyler's own journey. We don't judge Tyler for selling the card - medical bills are very real, and perhaps he wanted to move on from that stage of his life - but we can't imagine owning it. It feels a bit strange to know that such a sentimental card is stowed away in a stranger's private collection.

Alt Art Gemini Elf T3-04

Worth $254,791

Back in 1999, Gemini Elf was the best level-four normal monster around thanks to its 1900 attack value. So though it's unplayable today, it was a landmark card in early Yugioh. That's likely why the 2001 Asian Championships featured the Alternate Artwork Gemini Elf T3-04 as its fourth-place prize card.

The Asian Championships tournament was held in Japan and only open to players in the Asian nations that had access to the OCG - remember, this was a year before the Trading Card Game was released in North America and the rest of the world. All five prize cards featured alternate artwork, a first for the game.

This version of Gemini Elf is rare and has plenty of historical value. These prize cards were presented to players by Kazuki Takahashi, the creator of Yugioh himself.

On May 8, 2024, trading card seller Vintage Card Japan announced via Twitter that it had sold a copy of the card privately for 40 million yen, roughly $254,791 by the exchange rate at the time. It's still only a Gemini Elf, but it's the most storied Gemini Elf ever printed.

Masahiro the Dark Clown Tournament Prize

Worth $173,923

Masahiro the Dark Clown is a quirky card with a strange history. It's one of three prize cards from Japan's 2001 Second National Tournament. First to third place winners were all awarded with a custom card featuring their literal face. Hence, this strange anime monstrosity was born.

The Second National Tournament Prize cards have a murky history. In a forum post from 2010, Konami's US head of development Kevin Tewart claimed the three cards were fake. However, the card was on the Restricted List for the OCG's 2010 World Championship Series, hinting at its authenticity.

Further authenticating the card is PSA, who seems to have graded exactly one copy. Presumably, it's this one that sold on eBay for almost $174,000 in September 2025.

Blue-Eyes White Dragon LOB 1st Edition

Worth $85,000

Blue-Eyes White Dragon might be the most popular Yugioh card of all time, even if it isn't the rarest. A heavyweight both in the early days of the trading card game and the original anime series, it's still sought after today, especially if it's an ultra-rare mint-condition copy, like the Blue-Eyes White Dragon LOB 1st Edition.

Released in the game's first expansion set, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon (LOB), this first-edition PSA 10 Gem Mint condition card sold at auction in October 2020 for an astounding $85,000 (£65,000).

Such rare copies don't always reach that lofty height. In September 2023, another Gem Mint 10 copy sold on auction house Goldins for $28,000, plus $5,600 buyer's premium - a comparative bargain.

This isn't the only valuable Blue-Eyes printing. Back in June 2021, a Chinese court suspended an auction after bidding spiraled up to a wild $13.4 million / £10.1 million, as people clambered to get their hands on an ultra-rare Blue-Eyes White Dragon with a 20th-anniversary card frame.

Crush Card Virus Shonen Jump Championship 2007

Worth $50,000

As the name implies, the Crush Card Virus Shonen Jump Championship 2007 was a prize card from a tournament that pre-dated (and was later replaced by) the Yugioh Championship Series. Originally, 40 copies of this rare Yugioh card were produced, before a further two were made for the SJC 2008 tournaments.

It's the scarcity of this card that makes it so valuable to collectors, more so than its functionality or popularity. In June 2020, a PSA 10 gem mint copy sold for $49,999 (£40,058.70) on eBay. Not bad for a card that spent most of its life sitting on the Yugioh banlist, before Konami rewrote its rules text.

Minerva, the Exalted Lightsworn 2015 Prize Card

Worth $34,800

An ultra-rare variant of Minerva, The Exalted Lightsworn was awarded as the first prize in national heats for the 2015 Yugioh World Championship Series. The distinction between this version and the cards given out for second and third place is very subtle: the golden lettering is all that separates it from its kindred.

One such card with an excellent condition score of 9.5 sold via Heritage Auctions on November 6 2021 for $34,800, followed in March 2022 by a 9.0 condition card that moved for $31,200. Minerva might not matter much in the meta these days, but this card remains iconic.

Cyber Dragon GX Toy Promo

Worth $30,500

Back when the GX anime first aired on American TV, Konami partnered up with toy maker Mattel to release a range of action figures. Available only from Sears stores, each toy was a popular Yugioh summon, and the packs came with a limited edition version of that monster's card. However, midway through the third series of toys, the accompanying 'MF03' series of cards was pulled from the product.

This meant that cards for monsters released towards the end of the run had particularly short supply, none more so than MF03-009 Cyber Dragon. For many years this promo card was practically a myth: although it was listed in official guides to published cards, there were no photos of it in the wild.

That was until 2020, when redditor loserchris (real name Kevin, no surname given) shared the news on the r/yugioh subreddit that he had found several MF03 series cards in his closet, saying "I don't even remember where I got them". The community was flabbergasted that an MF03-009 was tucked among them.

Kevin sold the Cyber Dragon via an auction on the YGOrganization Discord, and confirmed to Wargamer that he received a tidy $30,500 for the card.

Cyber-Stein Shonen Jump Championship 2004

Worth $30,100

This copy of Cyber-Stein was originally awarded as a prize card at the Shonen Jump Championships between 2004 and 2005. Only 18 copies of the valuablye card were produced for the tournaments, although an extra two were printed for the tournaments in 2008, and 126 copies were made for a promotional event in 2009.

Regardless of its reprints, this is still a rare Yugioh card. A PSA 10 gem mint condition copy printed in the original 2004 auctioned in October 2020 for $30,100 (£22,800).

KC Grand Tournament 2nd Place Dark Magician

Worth $30,000

During the Coronavirus pandemic, Konami wisely suspended the World Championship for its mobile game Yugioh Duel Links, and in 2020 to 2022 it hosted the purely digital Kaiba Corporation Grand Tournament as a replacement. The prizes for the 2021 championship were trophy blocks containing Ultra Secret Rare printings of Dark Magician, which have no foiling on the Wizard's robes.

2021's second place finalist didn't hang onto their card for long, selling it via Heritage Auctions on December 2, 2022, where it sold for $32,000 plus $6,400 buyer's premium. The same card sold again via the same auction house almost exactly two years later, this time only hitting $30,000 (plus a larger $7,500 buyer's premium) on December 6 2024.

Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth Dark Duel Stories Promo

Worth $30,000

This little insect doesn't have much renown in the TCG community, but Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth made a name for itself as a valuable Yugioh card in August 2021. That's when a rare promo version of the card, released alongside the Dark Duels Stories Game Boy cartridge, that had been rated PSA 10 gem mint condition sold on eBay for a whopping $29,999.99 (£22,700).

At the time of its listing, it was billed as the only gem mint copy of the promo card in the entire world, making it somewhat unique. Since then, however, trading card authenticator and grading company PSA has listed three other copies of the card.

The Seal of Orichalcos UDE Event

Worth $26,400

The Seal of Orichalcos has appeared in several Yugioh sets, but that wasn't always the case. When it debuted in season four of the Yugioh anime in 2005, it had no paper counterpart. Upper Deck Entertainment decided to make their own custom version of the card.

This rare Yugioh card appeared only in UDE-organised "Duel the Master" side-events at tournaments. These were challenge games played against a master player, usually a judge, who wielded a stacked deck full of powerful cards.

The Seal of Orichalcos isn't really a promo, since it wasn't intended to make its way into the hands of players, and was never legal in any form of tournament play. This version of the card has an ominous final clause - if you lose against its owner, your soul is forfeit! Legend has it that only fifteen copies of the card were ever printed, suggesting it is one of the rarest cards in any TCG.

In 2017, Yu-Gi-Oh! collector Anthony Nguyen released a YouTube video revealing he'd acquired a copy of the legendary card. Once it became apparent that it was possible for collectors to get their hands on it, there were a spate of sales - with a 7-graded copy selling via Heritage Auctions for $26,400.

Blue-Eyes White Dragon Dark Duel Stories Promo

Worth $25,100

Another entry for the pallid serpent, this was one of six Prismatic Secret Rare cards released in promotion for the Yugioh Dark Duel Stories videogame. Two sets were created and were packaged inside the Gameboy game. One set contained ol' Blue-Eyes White Dragon, Exodia, and Dark Magician; the other had Acid Trap Hole, Seiyaryu, and Salamandra.

This PSA 10 gem mint condition copy sold at auction in February 2021 for the not-insignificant sum of $25,100 (£19,000). Although a fair few prismatic Blue-Eyes White Dragons made their way into the world as promo cards for the videogame, few have been kept in such great condition.

Chaos Emperor, the Dragon of Armageddon Prize Card

Worth $18,000

Chaos Emperor, the Dragon of Armageddon was a prize in the 2018 Yugioh Championship series. Championship winners were the first to get their hands on the powerful dragon, two years before its was available to the rest of the world in Battles of Legend Armageddon.

While it requires a lot of reading, this expensive Yugioh card has some pretty explosive effects. You can wipe out your opponent's board and their life points with its unique monster effect, or play it to either pendulum zone to retrieve another dragon from your graveyard. A copy of the ultra-rare first-place winner's card with a PSA Mint 9 rating sold via Heritage auctions for $18,000 in November 2021.

Dark Magician LOB 1st Edition

Worth $17,924

Another staple of the Yugioh anime and trading card game, Dark Magician is best known as the favorite card of protagonist Yugi Muto. And with that fame comes expense. Aa PSA 10 gem mint condition Dark Magician LOB 1st Edition, printed in the Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon set, was auctioned in July 2021 for $17,924 (£14,163).

Supposedly, the price of this card can climb even higher. Dicebreaker reported that, in June 2021, an Arkana variant (with a red background behind the magician) sold on eBay for a whopping $85,000. However, we've not seen a sale since then that's come anywhere close to such a price - though almost $20,000 for a single card is still excellent value indeed.

Card of Sanctity Kids WB Promo

Worth $17,000

This very valuable Yugioh card went for $17,000 plus buyer's premium on the auction site Goldin in April 2024. It's a special promo card that was given away by Kids WB in a tie-in with the Yugioh anime. The episode 'Back to Battle City Part 3' included instructions for US kids to enter a sweepstakes, and 100 winners received this special Card of Sanctity.

Naturally those priceless prizes were stuffed into drawers, traded away on the playground, bent, torn, or left outside in the rain. The $17,000 copy that sold at Goldins only has a PSA 8 Near Mint grade: there are basically no higher-quality versions of the card available.

It's worth noting that this card is a lot less powerful than the version in the anime, where it made each player draw up to six cards in their hand.

Doomcaliber Knight Shonen Jump Championship 2008

Worth $15,300

This copy of Doomcaliber Knight was handed to winners of the 2008 Shonen Jump Championships. Only 68 copies of the cards were ever produced.

In March 2021, a PSA 7 near-mint copy of the card was auctioned for $15,300 (£12,258.21). This is one of very few cards on this list that isn't graded PSA 10 - and since a copy has never been sold in PSA 10 condition, it's hard to know if they exist at all. The fact that copies sell for such high prices without a perfect grading goes to show how valuable the card is.

Morphing Jar Tournament Pack 2 Promo

Worth $15,000

Another promotional card, this copy of Morphing Jar was released in the second season Tournament Pack, a specially-compiled booster that was released at select tournament locations in late 2002. More than that, Morphing Jar was the pack's single Ultra Rare, making it doubly golden - and a pretty valuable card on the secondary market.

In Early 2021, a PSA 10 gem mint condition copy of the card sold for just under $15,000 (£12,000). Though we still think that Pot of Greed is the best piece of crockery to ever make its way into Yugioh.

Corrected Art Dark Paladin 1st Edition

Worth $15,000

Often, when a trading card gets misprinted, its recipient's dismay turns to glee when they realize their misshapen playing piece is now a rare collector's item. But in the case of Dark Paladin, it's the 'correction' to that misprint that now holds immense value.

The first edition English printing of Dark Paladin from the 2003 Yugioh set Magician's Force used the incorrect artwork. Upper Deck Entertainment, the distributor for English-language Yugioh cards in the 2000s, corrected the mistake for later editions of the card. But it also offered players with the misprinted card a chance to swap their 1st edition Dark Paladins for 1st edition Dark Paladins with the corrected art.

The offer was advertised on Upper Deck's website, and in various magazines. But it seems like many fans either didn't hear about it, didn't bother to send off for the card, or thought the misprint would be more valuable in the long run. Very few copies were put into circulation - and now the corrected art version of the Dark Paladin is much rarer and more expensive.

The highest recent price we could find was a PSA-graded gem mint condition copy that sold for $15,000 on Fanatics Collect on May 11, 2021. Props go to the Reddit user AzulRyu who documented this bit of TCG history in exhaustive detail.

German Pharaoh's Tour Prize Gold Sarcophagus

Worth $14,999

Another championship prize card, Gold Sarcophagus was the prize for national winners in the 2007 Pharoah's Tour series. The Ultra-Rare variant was awarded to first-place winners. Copies are extremely scarce, and this PSA 9-graded copy that sold in October 2025 is the only known copy of this grading.

Dark Magician Girl 1st Edition

Worth $13,200

Dark Magician Girl was first printed in 2003, in the North-America only set Magician's Force. Although she's had a wider reprint since then, this was the only printing to feature the card art used in the Yugioh anime.

A gem mint first edition Dark Magician girl sold for $9,100 via eBay in November 2020, while another sold for $13,200 via PWCC marketplace in July 2022. The deck archetype this expensive Yugioh card belongs to no longer sees much success at tournaments, but its rarity and the iconic status of the card keep its value high.

T.G. Hyper Librarian

Worth $11,250

Another tournament prize card, T.G. Hyper Librarian was given out as an exclusive never-before-seen card in 2011 to those who qualified in the National Championships to go on and take part in the World Championship series.

As that year's World Championships had 26 participants, that means that only 26 copies of this card were made. T.G. Hyper Librarian would only be a mechanically exclusive card for a year, as it got a wider printing in the 2012 set Return of the Duelist Special Edition. But that didn't quash the value of the original prize cards: a PSA 10 copy fetched $11,250 on Heritage Auctions in December 2024.

Red-Eyes Black Dragon LOB 1st Edition

Worth $10,600

Another favorite from Yugioh's line of vivid drakes with notable eye colors, Red-Eyes Black Dragon doesn't have the acclaim or market value of its esteemed Blue-eyed counterpart, but can certainly hold its own. One of ten Ultra Rares included in the first Yugioh set release, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon, this card was a prize to find.

Twenty years later, that prize has only gone up in value. A PSA 10 gem mint condition copy of the first-edition card cards for $10,600 (£8,000) in January 2021. Yugioh players sure do like their dragons.

Number 89: Diablosis the Mind Hacker Championship 2017

Worth $10,500

Number 89: Diablosis the Mindhacker was an exclusive card given to Yugioh Championship Series winners in 2017. The average duellist then had to wait four years for it to get a regular release in the 2021 set Brothers of Legend.

Most valuable Yugioh cards are rare but not powerful, but Diablosis is both. Its ability to banish cards from the opponent's extra deck, graveyard, and the top of their deck made it a disrupting terror in recent times, forcing many players to warp their deck-building process in an effort to counter it.

Fortunately, the aggrieved fans' prayers were answered when, in June 2023, the card was stuck onto the Yugioh banlist. It found its way to the Yugioh Master Duel banlist soon afterwards, in October.

Getting plenty of play will probably have boosted its market value at least a little, but ultimately it's the low supply, inherent to any prize card, that has made Diablosis so expensive. According to Heritage Auctions, which oversaw the sale of a copy for $10,500 in September 2022, only nine PSA 10 copies are known to exist.

Gaia the Dragon Champion 1st Edition

Worth $9,900

One of only two Secret Rare cards released in the very first Yugioh set, Gaia the Dragon Champion depicts a terrifying fusion between Gaia the Fierce Knight and Curse of Dragon. Terrifying in appearance, that is; with no abilities and mediocre stats, this warrior wouldn't stand a chance in the modern TCG meta.

You might think being one of the two rarest cards in the earliest Yugioh set would be enough to explain Gaia's high price, with a copy selling on Heritage Auctions for $9,9000 in 2021. However, the other Secret Rare card from the set, Tri-Horned Dragon, commands a pitiful price in comparison, of just a few hundred dollars.

Just like other more common and yet more expensive Legend of Blue Eyes cards such as Dark Magician and Blue-Eyes itself, it seems it is prestige that accounts for the difference. Gaia the Dragon Champion is a far more popular card than Tri-Horned Dragon, appearing in the anime's fifth episode, getting more reprints and appearing in more video games than its less appealing horny lizard friend.

Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon Retro Pack 2

Worth $9,000

Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon is one of nine Secret Rares from Retro Pack 2, with a bit of extra prestige thanks to the Blue-Eyes connection. The original limited edition printing of this card was given to kids who saw the 2004 movie, Yugioh: Pyramid of Light, in theaters. But it's actually this unlimited reprint from a few years later (2009) that's most expensive.

That's because, even though it's 'just' a reprint set, Retro Pack 2 had an extremely low print run and was very hard to get hold of in America. Boxes were released only in Europe, and now easily sell for over $5,000.

Less perfect copies of this exact card can be found online for $1000 - $2000, but the most staggering sale we found was a PSA 10 Gem Mint specimen that sold via Fanatics Collect in February 2021 for $9,000.

There's a funny bit of trivia about this card. You have to tribute Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon to summon Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon - but the Ultimate Dragon wasn't released until almost two years after the Shining Dragons's first printing, meaning this iconic dragon was completely unusable! D'oh!

Gladiator's Assault Magic Formula

Worth $8,700

When Magic Formula was printed in the 2007 set Gladiator's Assault, it became a key part of Dark Magician decks, offering power boosts to either Dark Magician or Dark Magician Girl, and a handy life boost should it go to the graveyard. The problem for duellists was getting their hands on it.

Gladiator's Assault was stuffed with secret rare cards and had a legendarily bad ratio of rare cards to commons and uncommons. Magic Formula was incredibly scarce, and copies from that first printing are still highly sought after: a gem mint Gladiator's Assault Magic Formula sold for $8,700 on PWCC marketplace in July 2022.

Exodia Legend Of Blue Eyes White Dragon 1st Edition

Worth $8,000

The notorious Exodia is just as prized on the collector's market as it is by duelists in the Yugioh anime. It's the ultimate monster, created by combining five Exodia cards into a single, unmatched entity: the Forbidden One. It's so powerful, in fact, that it grants its summoner immediate victory. No wonder that sniveling Weevil Underwood threw all of Yugi's Exodia cards off the boat in the first season.

This copy of Exodia is particularly prized for being a first-edition version that was printed in the game's original set from 2002, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon. It sold for $8,000 (£6,050), thanks no doubt to being graded at PSA 10 Mint Gem condition.

Attack of the Giant Card!! Cyber Dragon

Price Unconfirmed

In addition to being one of the most expensive Yugioh cards ever sold, the Attack of the Giant Card!! Cyber Dragon is also one of the biggest. 'Attack of the Giant Card!!' is an official tournament that rewards its winner with a Yugioh card that's around a meter tall.

According to an eBay listing, this giant Cyber Dragon was awarded at the Remote Duel Extravaganza in June 2022 as part of the Attack of the Giant Card!! Speed Duel tournament. Though we don't know the official offer accepted, the seller's OG asking price was just under $10,000 (£9,000) - so the final price is somewhere in this eye-watering ballpark.

Stainless Steel Black Luster Soldier

Rumored to be worth millions

Believed to have been awarded in Yugioh's first-ever national tournament in 1999, this curious card might be the most expensive Yugioh card of all time. Made of stainless steel, the unique one-of-a-kind Black Luster Soldier monster works differently to every other version of the card - since it's a Normal Monster, not a Ritual Monster.

According to Kotaku, the card was listed for sale for around $10 million back in 2013, but there's no indication it sold for that value. Elsewhere, a figure of $2 million is widely circulated, but this does not seem to have a verifiable source attached.

The above image is not the metal monster, but a paper duplicate of the card. 3,000 copies were released in June 2023 as a special promotion in Japan, to mark the 25th anniversary of the game.

How we check Yugioh card prices

Our guide is based on the highest prices each rare Yugioh card has fetched in sales we can verify. Every month, we review the most recent verified sales at various major online auction houses for collectibles, such as Goldin Auctions, Fanatics Collect, and Heritage Auctions. If a new sale beats a record, it makes the list. We also trawl eBay listings, but these sales are much more difficult to verify, and we'll never list a card's sale value unless we're satisfied the details are completely accurate.

There are cards that have been offered at higher prices, like the Blue Eyes Ultimate Dragon from the 2001 Asian Championships, but these don't have verified sales. The one exception on our list is the Stainless Steel Black Luster Soldier: this has never been sold, but it is such a renowned card that if it ever went to auction it would certainly become one of the most expensive Yugioh cards of all time.

For more costly trading cards, check out our guides to the most expensive MTG cards, and the most expensive Lorcana cards in Disney's TCG.

Epic Games Pivots to “AI-First” Coding Model for Future Games

Epic Games, despite being one of the most influential and well-known developers on the planet thanks to the superhit Fortnite, is not content to sit on its haunches and reap in more money than the GDP of a small country. For better or worse, the company has consistently felt the need to push the envelope on new ways they can make even fatter stacks of cash, and this latest effort is one of their most troubling ideas yet. A report from Jason Schreier on Monday revealed that Epic is pivoting hard into AI development principles, to the point that it seems to have delayed one of its biggest unannounced games. 

According to Schreier's sources, Epic’s been quietly working on a currently unannounced crossover shooter between the Disney and Marvel universes that was originally scheduled for March. However, development on the project was proceeding slower than executives had hoped, due to leadership underestimating the staff needed to create the game. To combat this, Epic Games leadership announced in a call to the team that the development of the unannounced shooter would now use an “AI-First” model, prioritizing at all levels using content and code created by artificial intelligence rather than by hand.

“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” Jake Jones, Epic’s Communications Director, told Schreier. Sources within Epic told Schreier that this meant leaning on AI almost completely for the development of the title, running everything through Anthropic’s Claude AI and with one employee even claiming that one leader told them “No more hand-written code.”

While Epic has previously been a big push for AI usage in games development, alongside several other major studios, this is the first major instance of a company utilizing complete AI dependence on a project of this scale. 

Disney has not made any comment at time of writing.

Credit: United Wizards of the Coast

Wizards of the Coast D&D and Magic Team Unionize

While the executives at Epic Games are trying to yank work away from its teams, the employees at Wizards are fighting hard to yank their work back. The Wizards of the Coast teams behind Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering are taking a cue from the Arena development team and announced their intent to unionize publicly last Tuesday. 

Organizing under the title United Wizards of the Coast (UWOTC), the Union wrote on Oct. 6th that, “As of this morning, both the Dungeons & Dragons team (which includes the workers behind Dungeons & Dragons and D&D Beyond) and Studio X (which includes the tabletop Magic: The Gathering and Duel Masters teams) informed Wizards of the Coast leadership of our intent to unionize, and called on the company to voluntarily recognize our union.” 

“The games we create are foundations of the gaming industry. Just as D&D has inspired countless TTRPGs and Magic sparked the TCG revolution, we hope to catalyze real change within our industry and build upon the groundwork laid by other gaming unions, creating a space where all workers are protected and treated fairly.”

UWOTC listed out a number of the issues that it’s fighting for, including protections against AI, job security against layoffs, sustainable workplace practices including access to remote and hybrid work, and full ownership of anything created by Wizards employees while off the clock. 

The UWOTC team publicly requested for the leadership at both Wizards and Hasbro, its parent company, to voluntarily recognize their union by October 13th, and failing this will start the union election process at Wizards. The D&D and Magic teams follow closely in the steps of the MTG Arena team, who successfully unionized and passed their own union vote earlier this year to create the UWOTC.

Credit: Games Workshop/Wizards of the Coast

Warhammer 40K Commander Decks Receives a Hotly Anticipated Second Printing

It’s a big week for Wizards in the roundup, and technically a big week for crossovers as well. Alongside the marquee announcement at NYCC for the upcoming Marvel: Darkhold Universes Beyond set, Wizards also quietly confirmed one of it’s other major crossovers, the fan favorite Warhammer 40,000 Commander decks, will be returning for a limited reprint run.

IGN broke the news last week after rumors began to surface from various game store employees who claimed that they were suddenly able to order the much sought after 40k Commander decks again. 

"Yes, we can confirm that we did a small reprint of the Commander decks that will be available to distributors and stores soon,” a Wizards of the Coast spokesperson told IGN. “Fans and WPN retailers should check with their distributors for availability, as it may vary by region."

This directly contradicts the earlier statement by Magic’s head designer, Mark Rosewater, where he wrote in a blog post in 2022 that, “There are no current plans to make in-universe Magic versions of the new cards in the Warhammer 40K Commander decks (we make in-universe ones for the Secret Lair cards), but we have the capability to do it if needed on a card-by-card basis.”

The four decks, originally released in October of 2022, each focus on one of the major factions of 40k, led by one of its iconic characters. This includes an Imperium deck with Inquisitor Greyfax as the Commander, a Chaos Deck with Abaddon, a Necron deck commanded by the Silent King, and a Tyranid deck under the control of the Swarmlord. 

No exact date has been given at this time as to when these decks will become available in stores again, in what quantity they will be made available, or if Wizards plans to do this with any of it’s other limited run Commander decks in the future.  

Credit: Disney/EA/Bit Reactor

Star Wars: Zero Company Developers Begin to Bring Back Furloughed Staff

A minor miracle is happening in the roundup this week. Instead of more people losing their jobs in the video game industry, just this once, dear reader, people are getting their jobs back.

After the crushing news earlier this year that Bit Reactor, the team behind the surprise hit Star Wars: Zero Company, was forced to furlough most of its staff prior to the games release, the studio put out a statement telling fans that thanks to their support of the game, they’ve been able to begin the process of bringing their employees back.

Greg Foertsch, the CEO of Bit Reactor, wrote in a statement posted to the company's Bluesky account that, “This week, we started the process of returning more of our team back to work at Bit Reactor, an important step forward in our continued support of Zero Company.”

Foertsch continued by writing, “Having to ask team members to step away after we navigated unexpected business developments outside of our control so close to launch was an incredibly difficult decision, but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible.”

The statement does not confirm the exact number of employees who have been able to return to work, a report from Game File claims that over half of the staff initially furloughed have returned, though the exact numbers remain undisclosed. Bit Reactor will likely need to publicly report those still affected by the mass furlough should any of them remain off the payroll for longer than six months, and so far only two months have passed. 

“This team means a tremendous amount to me, and I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished together,” Foertsch writes at the end of his statement. “Thank you to our fans for the incredible response to the game and for supporting us along this journey. We look forward to sharing more updates regarding Bit Reactor and Zero Company soon.”

Credit: Hasbro

Hasbro Expands Partnership with Renegade Game Studios 

Hasbro is closing us out this week on the roundup, which means since it’s the parent company of Wizards of the Coast Hasbro gets to enjoy a Tabletop Battles Industry News Roundup hat trick. This time though, rather than Wizards of the Coast in the spotlight for Hasbro, it's Renegade Game Studios, as Hasbro and Renegade announced its contract extension with the company as it continues to push into the tabletop industry.

"We’re extremely pleased to extend and expand our relationship with Hasbro,” said Scott Gaeta, President of Renegade, in the press release for the agreement. “From our beginnings with Power Rangers to our most recent projects on Dungeons & Dragons Lords of Waterdeep, working with the teams at Hasbro and Wizards of the Coast has been a pleasure. It’s an honor to be entrusted with bringing these iconic brands to tabletops worldwide.”

Hasbro and Renegade first partnered in 2018 to contract Renegade to create tabletop games based on the Power Rangers franchise, and has since then entrusted the company with several of its top dollar tabletop game licenses including Axis and Allies, Diplomacy, Robo Rally, and Heroscape. It’s even brought Renegade in to collaborate with Wizards on games based on the Dungeons and Dragons IP, such as Lords of Waterdeep.

While the announcement of the agreement only specifies that it will last “through 2027 and beyond”, the success that the partnership has brought for both companies thus far likely means that this relationship will continue to strengthen as Hasbro tries to carve out more space for itself in the tabletop board game world.

title: DnD stats explained in simple language
content:
When you want to sling a spell, dodge a blow, or fell a foe, it's the six basic Dungeons and Dragons stats that decide your fate. Every time you roll a D20 to take an action, one of your character's fundamental stats (a.k.a. ability scores) comes into play - sometimes saving you from a bad roll, sometimes dooming you in spite of a good one. Understanding how DnD stats work is crucial to the whole game - and this simple guide will teach you everything you need to know.

Alright, let's start simple. The six DnD stats are Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. You decide the starting value of these 'ability scores' during character creation, but they can be modified by certain character options (DnD races in 5e, for example, or DnD backgrounds in 5.5e - check out the linked guides to learn more).

Your ability scores are split into physical and mental stats. This classic Tumblr post gives an excellent description of what each of the stats allows a character to do, in terms of a tomato:

  • Strength - helps you crush a tomato.
  • Dexterity - helps you catch a thrown tomato.
  • Constitution - helps you eat a bad tomato and not get sick.
  • Intelligence - helps you understand why a tomato is a fruit.
  • Wisdom - helps you recognize that a tomato shouldn't be in a fruit salad.
  • Charisma - helps you to sell a fruit salad made of tomatoes by marketing it as salsa.

The higher your ability score, the better you are at getting things done. Higher ability scores have higher ability score modifiers, and it's the modifiers you get to add to rolls of your D20.

Ability ScoreAbility Modifier
1- 5
2-3- 4
4-5- 3
6-7- 2
8-9- 1
10-11+0
12-13+1
14-15+2
16-17+3
18-19+4
20-21+5
22-23+6
24-25+7
26-27+8
28-29+9
30+10

Some stats also modify other parts of your character which aren't used for rolls. For example, your Strength modifier decides your character's carrying capacity, while Constitution affects your hit point maximum.

Strength

Strength is a specialist skill in D&D. Unless you plan to swing a sword (or greathammer, or almost any other melee weapon), you probably don't need it. Sure, it makes you great at Athletics, and it increases your carrying capacity. But these aren't a high priority for anyone except Bob the Barbarian.

Dexterity

Dexterity is, in my opinion, the unsung hero of D&D stats. It can do almost everything Strength can, provided you're okay with Finesse weapons only. It also allows you to use ranged weapons, and it boosts your armor class. That last one is crucial for almost any character. Dexterity-based martial characters are among the strongest character builds. And, when a spellcaster needs extra defense, they reach for Dexterity, not Strength.

Constitution

Constitution gives you the fewest benefits of any stat, but it's oddly more important than any other. Constitution decides your hit point maximum, which decides how many hits you take before you're dead. In a combat-focused campaign, nothing is more important than that number. Plus, Constitution decides how well you maintain concentration on spells - and that's pretty darn essential for magic users.

Intelligence

 

Wisdom

Wisdom is the spellcasting ability of choice for Clerics, Druids, and Rangers. Monks also use it to power their focus abilities. While that makes it those class' top priority, plenty of other characters benefit from Wisdom, too. It fuels skills like Survival and Perception (in my opinion, some of the most important skills in the game). Plus, Wisdom saving throws are incredibly common, so a high score in this stat protects you from enemy spellcasters.

Charisma

Charisma represents both divine power and a gift of the gab. By that, I mean it's the spellcasting ability for Bards, Sorcerers, Warlocks, and Paladins alike. Naturally, it's also the fuel for all your social interactions. If you want your character to be as smooth a talker as you are in real life, you better boost their Charisma score.

How to pick stats

When deciding how to pick stats for your character, start by prioritizing your 'primary ability score'. The Player's Handbook lists a key ability score for each class. This is usually your spellcasting ability or, if you can't use magic, your main method of attack.

Most classes only rely on a single stat to function. We call this SAD (Single Ability Score Dependent). For example, a Wizard only really needs a high Intelligence to be good at casting spells.

For SAD characters, your second stat to focus on is usually Constitution. This boosts your maximum hit points and your ability to concentrate on spells, so it's key to the survival of pretty much any character.

For some classes, there is an argument for making Dexterity your second-most important stat. This increases your armor class, so it's handy for defense. It's also tied to a lot more useful skills than Constitution.

Not every class is SAD, though. At the other end of the scale are MAD (Multiple Ability Score Dependent) characters. These classes must focus on two or more stats in order to excel. For example, a Paladin uses Charisma for spellcasting, but they also need a high Strength score for smites. Similarly, a Monk fuels their Focus with Wisdom, but they'll need Dexterity for attacking and defending in melee.

In this case, some players aim to increase these stats at an equal pace. Others prefer to lean more heavily on one than the other. A Paladin that doesn't do too much spellcasting with Charisma is still perfectly playable as long as you build around their Strength score.

MAD characters still benefit from high Constitution or Dexterity scores, but these become tougher to prioritize when you want to juggle more than one primary Ability Score.

How to calculate DnD stats

The three methods of calculating your base DnD stats are:

  1. Rolling
  2. Standard array
  3. Points buy (27 rule)

How do you roll for DnD stats?

To roll for a character's stats, roll 4D6, remove the lowest die result, and note the total. Do this six times to generate six numbers between three and 18, then assign each of these numbers to one of your stats. Voila! You have your base stats, ready to add any bonuses from your character's race.

Randomly rolled stats can have more extreme results than other methods, but it's the only way to get a base stat above 15 (before you add bonuses). It's generally favored by players that enjoy exploring characters' big weaknesses - because you could well end up with some stats so low you'll take a minus two or minus three to your roll every time you use them!

What is standard array?

Standard array is a fixed set of base stats: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8. You will use each number in the array for one stat. It's equivalent to making average dice rolls, or building a balanced character with points buy.

The main advantages of using the standard array system are speed and reliability. There's no random chance involved - you can simply plop the bigger scores onto the most important stats for your chosen class, giving your a character a basic statline that's optimized for the type of role you're intending to play in the party, but also balanced across other stats. Most importantly, you'll only have one true 'dump' stat below ten.

On the downside, of course, you won't have any truly excellent ability scores. Not only is it impossible to get any ability score higher than 15, but you'll only have one stat at 15. By rolling for stats, you could end up with 18s for everything - so the question is: are you feeling lucky, punk?

How does the points buy system work?

The points buy system gives you 27 points to spend on your stats, with each stat value costing a fixed number of points. This is sometimes called the D&D '27 rule'.

StatCost
80
91
102
113
124
135
147
159

The points buy system is the most fiddly way to calculate stats, but it gives you the most control over your character's core abilities.

How to increase DnD stats

The main way to get better stats is to level up! At certain stages of play, you'll get the chance to choose an Ability Score Increase. Alternatively, you can pick another general feat that gives you a less impressive stat boost (along with another cool ability).

Most classes get stat improvements at fourth, eighth, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, but the Fighter and Rogue both also receive stat improvements at sixth and 14th level. A multiclass character does not gain stat improvements based on its overall level, but on each class level separately - so a second-level Fighter / second-level Wizard would not receive a stat improvement.

The only other way to fiddle with your scores after character creation is magic items. These can even get your stats past 20 - something regular Ability Score Increases can't offer!

The most impactful of these items are the infamous, single-use Tomes and Manuals, each of which permanently increases a given stat by 2. All are Very Rare, Wondrous Items that you should expect to find very occasionally. You'll need to study the book for 48 hours over a period of six days to get the effect - after that it can be used again, but only after a century.

These items are:

  • Manual of Gainful Exercise - increase STR by 2
  • Manual of Quickness of Action - increase DEX by 2
  • Manual of Bodily Health - increase CON by 2
  • Tome of Clear Thought - increase INT by 2
  • Tome of Understanding - increase WIS by 2
  • Tome of Leadership and Influence - increase CHA by 2

Beyond that, there are a variety of magic items that grant you buffs to stats only while you have them equipped.

These are also all very rare, but the most commonly seen are:

  • Ioun Stones - Small stones that float around your head, conferring +2 to a given stat, depending on the type of stone - to a maximum of 20. Others can give temporary bonuses to AC, Proficiency Bonus, and more.
  • Belt of Dwarvenkind - Increases CON by 2 to a maximum of 20. Also gives you 60ft of Darkvision, resistance to poison and Advantage on saves against poisoned, makes you better at persuading Dwarves, and gives you a 50% chance of growing a beard every day.
  • Gauntlets of Ogre power - Sets your STR to 19 exactly, but has no effect if you're already at 19 or higher.
  • Belt of Giant Strength - Sets your STR to a given total between 21 and 29, depending on the type of Giant.
  • Amulet of Health - Sets your CON to 19 exactly, but has no effect if you're already at 19 or higher.
  • Headband of Intellect - Sets your INT to 19 exactly, but has no effect if you're already at 19 or higher.

Got any more rules questions? Ask us any time in the Wargamer Discord.
