title: Hunt for Blackbeard is a thrilling board game about myth, history, deception, and piracy
content:
Our Verdict

Hunt for Blackbeard is a tense, thematic game of hidden movement. Its efficient, effectively-chosen mechanics allow you to hunt down Blackbeard while also detangling his real history from the myths that surround him. Lovers of history and narrative design will relish the authentic choices made here, though the reliance on luck may mean it's less esteemed by lovers of flawless strategy.

Pros
  • Extremely thematic
  • Tense and exciting
  • Lovely components
Cons
  • Relies heavily on luck
  • Not especially innovative

Everything you know about Blackbeard is, probably, wrong. Captain Edward Thatch's career of piracy has been glamourised so extensively that even historians often struggle to separate fact from fiction. Every aspect of his life has been embellished, from birth to death. This sensational legacy gives you ideas about what a Blackbeard board gameshould look like.

You're probably making assumptions right now. Blackbeard's name brings to mind explosive naval battles and glittering buried treasure. Park those assumptions for a moment, because they're wrong.

Hunt for Blackbeard is a two-player hidden movement game, designed by Volko Ruhnke and published by Fort Circle Games. It recreates the events that led to Blackbeard's final engagement, the fatal Battle of Ocracoke.

One player acts as Blackbeard and the crew aboard the ship Adventure. Their goal is to sail around North Carolina, continuing a life of piracy while evading capture. Their opponent plays members of the Royal Navy, employed to hunt Blackbeard on behalf of the colony of Virginia. Armed with two sloops and a single captain on foot, they must deduce where Blackbeard is hiding, then close in to apprehend him.

The rulebook bears an important subtitle: "Simulating the true events of 1718″. The Hunt for Blackbeard is a game of deduction in more ways than one. This isn't just a historic manhunt, remade in abstract with blocks and pawns. The players themselves are, turn by turn, deducing who Blackbeard really is.

Real people and events are cleverly scattered among the game's mechanics. The chase plays out on a cramped map of North Carolina, with different ports, towns, and seas represented by wooden blocks. These blocks face Blackbeard, concealing his camp and movements from the Navy player.

Each round, players draw a new tile that determines their actions and goals. The Navy player gains an informant, based on a real person, who lets them scout certain blocks in secret. The aim here is to find sightings of Adventure, Adventure itself, or the camp Blackbeard will likely retreat to.

Blackbeard, on the other hand, draws two tiles: an 'act of piracy' and a 'pirate's life'. The former represents the captain continuing his conquest. He might raid towns, recover loot at sea, stow booty, or even deal with conniving government figures.

Alternatively, Blackbeard can choose to pursue a quiet life, spending the fruits of his labor on spouses, crew, doctors, and rum. Life's simple pleasures, earned illegitimately.

There are only four rounds in Hunt for Blackbeard. If Blackbeard himself evades capture until the end of the fourth round, he can win by piracy. This only happens if the Blackbeard player filled at least half of one tile track with cubes. Fail to live either lifestyle to the fullest, and the Navy player wins by default.

Everything in this game is in short supply, though - money, turns, the pawns you spend on actions and movement. Every decision is crucial and cutthroat. If Blackbeard wants to win by piracy, he can't juggle both tile tracks. He must choose who to be.

The only alternative is to prepare for war. Either player can instead win by besting the other in combat. Both Blackbeard and the Navy can invest gold in outfitting their men, improving their chances to fire, board, or escape. Neither knows what the other has prepared, thanks to privacy screens that conceal each player's components.

Apprehending Blackbeard is the Navy player's best chance of success, but they have to find him first. Scouting, either with informants or by physically exploring the map, is costly and time-consuming. And even if you do find Blackbeard, there's always a chance he'll board and overwhelm you.

Attempts at arrest, whether they happen on land or at sea, are decided by a series of dice rolls. You roll to battle, then to escape, and then (if you don't want to escape) to board the enemy. Your preparations typically add or reduce dice on either side of the fight. Ultimately, though, you can only sway things so much - the end result remains random.

Board games are an interesting medium to explore history through. They present a reality in flux, where the victors of an exchange have not been decided. Blackbeard may, through a clever move or a lucky dice roll, survive the battle and go on pirating.

This subverts the facts, but what do facts matter to Blackbeard, anyway? Blackbeard the legend bears almost no resemblance to reality. His victory here only allows us to further warp Blackbeard's spotty biography.

A win for the Navy, meanwhile, cements the truth. Blackbeard was not an unstoppable force, gunned down in a climactic final fight. He was cornered, awaiting pardon, and wholly unequipped for the battle that would kill him. A historical supplement included with the game tells us the Battle of Ocracoke lasted about an hour. The hand-to-hand combat that killed Blackbeard happened in less than six minutes.

The dice roll that decides the game is mechanically anticlimactic. You can spend the whole game making clever bluffs and efficient maneuvers, only to have fate betray you at the last minute. It deflates the thrilling cat-and-mouse you'd been playing up until this point.

Thematically, though, it's a perfect choice. It captures the diceiness of a real naval battle. It also captures how disappointingly mundane Blackbeard's death was. Blackbeard may be a legend, but Edward Thatch was just a man.

Hunt for Blackbeard is an enjoyable, if not overly innovative, hidden movement game. Its brutal efficiency is often thrilling. Plus, impressively, it's a tense head-to-head that asks for less than an hour of your time. There are moments where its challenge feels unfair, as so much of the game hinges on tile draws and dice rolls. But, as a thematic experience and an artifact of history, it excels. It's one of the most memorable board games I've played this year.

Want to hear more about the year's best board games? Check out our dedicated guide, or ask for some recommendations in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Games Workshop seeks math-minded designer to make Warhammer 40k "fair, balanced, and enjoyable"
content:
Games Workshop is recruiting a new Technical Designer for Warhammer 40,000, a designer-cum-editor who will "be responsible for establishing quality standards by developing tools to improve efficiency, and ensuring the mathematical and logical robustness of our game mechanics". If you think you can do a better job making Warhammer 40,000 "fair, balanced, and enjoyable" than the hardworking designers at Games Workshop HQ have achieved so far, now's your opportunity to put your money where your mouth is.

According to the job description on the Warhammer careers website, the new post holder will be "responsible for the technical accuracy and integrity of our rules across all publications, from Codexes to balance updates to the Core Rules". As GW describes it, the role "is part rules editor, part tools developer, and part rules writer" who can "communicate complex mechanics with absolute clarity".

This responsibility cashes out in a variety of ways. The post-holder will "develop and contribute to our rules standards", which could refer to a style guide of official wording and terminology for the writing team, or to best-practise documents and reference materials that set parameters for how rules should be designed. With teams working on multiple Warhammer 40k codex releases simultaneously, that kind of documentation is necessary to keep everything standardized.

One task that falls to the Technical Designer is going to particularly interest fans: they will "develop and maintain points and efficiency calculations. While I dislike Games Workshop's policy of not naming the authors and artists who develop its books, I can well imagine the Technical Designer wanting anonymity. This post-holder could easily become the lightning rod for fan complaints any time the balance of Warhammer 40k is (or appears to be) out of whack.

While Games Workshop doesn't list many essential attributes for applicants, it looks like skill with data analysis and even computer coding will be valuable. The job description specifies the post-holder will "create automated testing and validation tools". On what platforms, and for what subjects, isn't specified. Maybe GW wants a tool that will speed up proof-reading; maybe the designers have asked for tools that will let them input hypothetical stats and get back charts about how units will perform; perhaps someone wants a way to simulate whole games of Warhammer 40k to brute-force data collection.

As is typical, Games Workshop does not list the remuneration for the role. Applicants must be able to work full time from Games Workshop's HQ in Nottingham, UK. The listing is open to applications until 5pm PDT / 8pm EDT / midnight GMT on Sunday October 25.

What would you do in this role? Have a chat in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Tabletop Battles in a Fantasy Jazz Age: Using Brutality Skirmish Wargame for Custom Games
content:
I have long been looking for a game with a "Fantasy Jazz Age" aesthetic - something like Shadowrun but set in the interwar years, the kind of striking style we got from Magic's New Capenna expansion, or Hearthstone's Mean Streets of Gadgetzan.

It's turned out harder than I expected. Sure, The Chicago Way offers a mechanically solid game to play out prohibition-era clashes, but it's somewhat lacking in a way to incorporate fantastical elements like different species of mobster, or spell-slinging.

Well, Brutality: Skirmish Wargame has that covered.

Scott Wainwright’s self-published rule set that advertises itself as a Versus / Solo / Co-op, Brutality is a miniatures agnostic game that lends itself well to both casual afternoon pickup games and dedicated campaigns lasting weeks - the perfect scale to represent gang warfare amidst mean streets!

(While Brutality does come with its own lore, covering a strange realm where the dead goddess Ishtar harvests energy from beings kidnapped from across time and space that are reborn the next day following death, it really shines when you take the toolbox of options it offers and make something you want!)

Who wouldn't want to make a deal with this guy? (Credit - hydriatus)

The Rules

The rules themselves are simple: Each player has a warband of between 4 and 8 models, with each model having a stat profile built by the players to represent anything from a medieval peasant with a pitchfork to an alien cyborg with a missile launcher - a wide range which easily provides for my requirement of "orc with a tommy gun", "dwarf bare-knuckle boxer", or "elf lounge singer with a literal magic voice".

A profile consists of the following stats:

  • Movement (how far a model can move in inches)
  • Fighting Skill (the physical melee skill of model)
  • Dexterity (the agility of a model, and it's passive defense against ranged attacks)
  • Hit Points (the amount of damage a model can take)
  • Willpower (the skill of a model to invoke Powers - magic or psychic as you prefer to flavor them)
  • Attacks (the amount of melee attacks a model can make)
  • Save (the model's ability to resist damage)

The game is written for 28/32mm figures, and includes a list of suggested base sizes as well for various profiles.

Unless stated otherwise by a scenario, a game lasts four turns on a 3' x 3' table. Each turn, players alternate activating one model until all have been activated. A model's activation is split into a movement phase and a combat phase, both of which have several options for actions a model can take.

During a movement phase, a model does one of the following:

  • Move
  • Stand Up
  • Pick Up a Dropped Weapon
  • Take Aim

During a combat phase, a model does one of the following:

  • Use Powers
  • Run
  • Interact with an Object
  • Staunching Bleeding
  • Stamp Out Flames
  • Use an Item
  • Shoot Ranged Weapons
  • Charge and Make Melee Attacks

Some actions resolve automatically (such as removing status tokens), and others (mostly attacks) require die rolls.

When rolling dice, players use a single D10 and attempt to roll equal or under a model's modified stats, with unmodified rolls of 1 being critical successes. Ranged attacks are an exception, as they use a number of dice depending on the weapon being used, and the die result has to be equal or more than the target's Dexterity stat.

If you're curious to delve deeper, a free version of the rules is available from the game's website, or through the game's Facebook group.

Campaign Play

Brutality comes with a simple but robust campaign system, which lasts until an agreed goal score is reached by one of the involved players, or an agreed amount of games has been played, at which point the player with the highest score is declared the winner.

The book provides 10 narrative missions, and 5 Solo/Co-op missions that can be played.

Since I wanted to test a variety of options and post-game consequences, I decided to run a short 3 game campaign, involving two gangs.

There is an expansion book that introduces Settlement Mode, which adds settlement development to the campaign structure. With it, you can chart the rise of a frontier outpost or survivor haven, and it includes rules for fighting over it when raiders or rival warbands come calling - which I can easily see forming the basis of a campaign to develop a neighborhood in my fledgling setting instead...

Making the Game Your Own

When it comes to building a list for a game of Brutality, it is easy to be somewhat intimidated by the sheer amount of options. There are no "pre-built" warbands or profiles, you have to build your own faction from the ground up. However, the rules to do so are actually quite straightforward.

Model profiles are created from simple archetypes, which you modify by boosting two stats and adding an ability from a list. There are also traits and Powers, to further differentiate models that share an archetype, and then there are also Faction Traits that apply abilities to all the models in a warband.

So here's how I went about making my own crews for a brief 3 game campaign covering a turf war:

  • The first thing I did was dig through my collection of suitable models to build two equal sized gangs.
  • Using the Profile creation rules, I generated stats for each model.
  • I picked out a Faction Trait to give both gangs some flavor.
  • Following a quick glance through the list of missions and my available scenery, I picked out three missions that could be strung together to tell an interesting narrative.

And just like that, I was ready to roll!

The Graveside Mob

Ruled by a lich dwelling deep in the City's necropolis, the Graveside Mob is made up mostly of the living, acting as the so-called public face of the necromantic cult warring for control of the criminal underworld. Their grim reputation of stashing contraband in graveyards and utilizing undead for labor has led to most folks keeping clear of any street bearing their mark. But they readily supply anyone who asks with anything they need, so their business has managed flourish despite their customers' misgivings.

Now, a high ranking cultist known as Lady Isabella has learned of an old relic being transported through Acacia Row, that could earn her great favor from the lich if it was to be secured...

The Graveside Mob (Credit - hydriatus)

As a starting campaign gang, the Graveside Mob is made up of the following five models:

  • Lady Isabella

    Support archetype, with Summoning, Curse, and Missile Powers.

  • Mr Vurbag

    Melee archetype, with the Sturdy ability.

  • Li'l Stoutsnout

    Fast archetype, with the Hidden ability.

  • Sean Kane

    Ranged archetype, with the Piercing ability.

  • Mo Heath

    Ranged archetype, with the Point Blank ability.

As known collaborators with the undead, the Mob has the Horror Faction trait.

The Quarry Lane Regulars

Named for a former rock quarry absorbed by the City's expansion, Quarry Lane is a single spiraling road leading to the base of an open pit which is home to the majority of hard-working souls. Since the outlawing of many vices that ease the burden of hard work, Quarry Lane has become one of the most lucrative territories a gang could control - after all, everyone knows the old saying about dwarves and ale! 

The Regulars are essentially a joint effort by various trade and labor unions based out of Quarry Lane to limit the influence of other criminal rackets who would exploit the situation... and the law enforcement who would stamp out all activities deemed illegal which make life bearable. To aid them in their desire for independence, the Regulars have learnt of a curious artifact being smuggled through Acacia Road - one worth a pretty penny or a dear favor to the right buyer, if they were able to acquire it...

The Quarry Lane Regulars (Credit - hydriatus)

As a starting gang, the Quarry Lane Regulars is made up of the following five models:

  • Dakdrul Bottlemace

    Melee archetype, with Clobber ability.

  • Gwinmyla Bottlemace

    Support archetype, with Devotion ability.

  • Mernan Barleystep

    Fast archetype, with Stealthy ability.

  • Higgins Bramblebelly

    Ranged archetype, with Sturdy ability.

  • Booker Oxton

    Ranged archetype, with Defensive Training ability.

A Golden Opportunity Campaign

With a pair of gangs picked out and balanced, it was time to come up with a basic story to string together a few games and explore the world through. A quick flick through the rulebook's scenarios, I decided on a classic "seize the artifact" story line. In between each mission, the gangs would go through a Home Phase, carrying out their upkeep as per the Campaign Rules in the book (so applying earned experience to models, resting to recover stat modifiers, or exploring their neighborhoods in pursuit of new members, rare items, or chance encounters).

The first scenario, Highwaymen, sees both gangs trying to rob a merchant and their cart, earning Victory Points for looting the cart and wounding the merchant. The victor of this scenario manages to seize the artifact, and transports it back to their base. As such, they become the Defender in the following mission.

The second scenario, Base Assault, is all about one gang trying to rob the enemy base. This audacious assault, driven by desperation, sees the Defenders re-spawning throughout the mission. However, as points are scored by booth looting Scavenge Points and killing enemies, this actually puts the Attackers at an advantage. The winner of this scenario is assumed to have secured the relic, and shipped it off immediately after to their patron/headquarters. Unfortunately, this angers the rival gang, who are automatically the Attackers in the final scenario.

The third and last scenario, Path of Destruction, sees the gang that lost the artifact decide to send a message in a spectacular fashion, attacking the territory of their rivals to make it clear they are not to be crossed. The Attackers earn Victory Points by killing Defenders, and destroying five Objectives scattered across the middle of the battlefield.

By the end of this starter campaign, one gang will have earned the favor/support of a patron, while the other would have triggered an all out gang war for the slight visited upon them. From there, a follow up campaign could involve the same gangs, or see new ones get drawn into the conflict and potentially escalate it further...

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: MTG Reality Fracture's Alchemy cards are so good they deserved to be in the main set
content:
Wizards of the Coast has begun to reveal Reality Fracture: Alchemy cards, the digital-only Magic: The Gathering format's final swan song before it is officially consigned to the scrap heap. And the more I see, the more I wish these were 'real' card designs, part of the set proper. We could've had an Urza-style Jace saga land, and a blue-white Quintorious? You can't see me, but imagine that I'm shaking my fist at the sky.

To some extent, this is nothing new. Players who don't partake in Alchemy have always lamented the locking away of cool card designs or character concepts into the Arena-only format. It doesn't help that it often seems like a regular Magic card was designed first and then the team found a way to 'Alchemize' it, giving it an effect that wouldn't work in paper.

But it's particularly noticeable this time around. Firstly because this is such a meaningful set, a huge Magic story moment and a love letter to the game's characters and settings - so the Alchemy cards are cooler than usual. And secondly, because Alchemy is going away so very soon, which means the addition of new cards feels (and this may seem a little harsh) a bit pointless.

The 'What If?' style echoverse characters are particularly upsetting to see in this form. I would love to play with an angel Valgavoth, or the color-swapped versions of the Strixhaven students, or a stegosaurus Etali that conjures forth random dinosaurs. But I'm not about to spend my wildcards on a ton of Alchemy cards for the privilege. Though, that said, I probably am going to boot up the format to try that ridiculous randomized planeswalker card.

At the end of the day, we non-Alchemy players should let the digital fans have their fun. We shouldn't bitch and moan. If Alchemy didn't exist I imagine these cards would not have found their way into the main set, they probably just wouldn't have been made. At least Alchemy gives us a way to see these ideas that might otherwise have been bound for the cutting room floor.

What I really long for, I suppose, is a return to blocks, for WotC to spend more than one set exploring an idea - when it merits it. It's still quite bizarre to me that the one experiment they did with this was for Innistrad, creating one set that focused slightly more on werewolves and one that focused slightly more on vampires (but both sets had plenty of both). That was not a good example of the sort of idea that deserves two sets!

Then again, with UB taking up one-half of the MTG release schedule, a return to blocks would mean spending an entire year in one place, and I'm not sure I'm up for that.

title: These Tag Team Pokemon cards are exploding in price - and they're not even that rare
content:
If you've got a binder full of rare Pokémon cards from the Sun & Moon era, now could be the time to re-evaluate what you're holding onto. Demand has been steadily growing for an overlooked class of cards: Tag Team Pokémon, characterful full art holo rares featuring two or more monsters fighting side by side, printed in 2019.

Tag Team cards appeared in four Pokémon sets, all from the Sun & Moon era: Team Up, Unbroken Bonds, Unified Minds, and Cosmic Eclipse. While sky-high prices for secret rares are completely expected, prices have surged on even the most basic, accessible printings of these Pokémon, including cards that were widely available in League Battle decks.

YouTuber PTCGRadio deserves the credit for pointing out this trend, and you can watch their video below for their analysis and discussion. They go into a lot of detail on specific cards.

29 Team Pokémon were printed as holo rares in mainline sets - almost all of them have gone up in price over the last year, and some of them have been growing fast. Here's how their market prices on TCG Player have changed since October 2025.

title: 40K Weekend Update: Battle for Salvation and Teams Results, Sam Pope Player Focus
content:
If you tuned in last week to see our Weekend Update article, welcome back. If you are just joining us, thanks for stopping by. This new series will cover the big events and stories that are happening each week in wargames, so you can stay updated and informed every week. The 40k side will be mostly covered by me, Isaac Terada, while Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson covers the non-40k side of event coverage and news.

John Lennon Wins Battle for Salvation

BFS was the largest event of the weekend with 131 players and 8 rounds, followed by Denver 40K Fight Club Oct. Open ‘26 with 104 players and 6 rounds. Events quickly drop off there in player size making this a pretty slow weekend for singles play. Both of the two large events were won by Space Marines; the first was taken by John with his combined Ultramarines and Deathwatch roster. Abusing the powerful melee threats in Assault Brethren combined with Calgar and the Deathwatch Terminators using their specialized Detachments, he was able to gun down the competition for a 7-1 finish. Notably, if you look at the event he was manually made #1. The head judge said that the X-1 and X-0 players going into day three agreed that whoever played on the top table round 8 would have spots 1 & 2 guaranteed to them even if they had a lower record. This was to make sure that even though there would be a single X-0 player after round 7 that anyone with a X-1 record could have a shot. That meant that while Sam Pope’s World Eaters went into round 7 as the only X-0 player, anyone who beat him would be able to take first, which John Lennon handily did, only losing to the Marines mirror versus Jack Murphy earlier in the event. 

Teams Back for a Big Weekend

Teams had a slow weekend last time we covered them, but this weekend they came back in a big way. Five teams events broke five rounds and over 100 players. The two largest were both six man teams, with an eight and two five-man roster events rounding up the top five. The rising number of events that aren’t just 8s and 5s is very interesting to see, and I am excited to see if 6s might become a new standard for smaller teams events outside of just European-run gigs. GT MADRID LETANIA DEL OSO was the largest event with 228 players split into six-man teams; congrats to Wargames Adictos for taking it down. Congratulations to Gonzalo "Raven" de La Moneda, Joker, Manu, Marco Esteban, Miguel Durá, & Terroxer El Rojo for the win with a 4-0-1 record. 

Deathwatch Terminators by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

First Codex Space Marines Results

The slate has finally taken over 40k events, no more stragglers with busted Orks. Now instead Space Marines have jumped into the lead. Funnily enough, Deathwatch has had a large influx of players, with 16 of them accounting for a 67% win rate. Does this have anything to do with any Marine army having access to 400 points of the best infantry shooting in the game if they bring Deathwatch terminator? Who can say. Orks still have a respectable 54% winrate, but no event wins, maybe they finally got hit enough to keep them out of top tables. 54% is still pretty high for a faction to hit this hard with the nerf bat so I would keep my eye on them. 

Most of the other event winners were spread across a decent selection of factions, but one to watch is World Eaters. They had a just-okay 51% winrate but took 8 players into a TiWP, which led to three undefeated finishes and a winner. They had the highest percentage of TiWP factions this weekend; those buffs on the last slate I think were just enough to push them into viability. If you want to learn how to deal with this new threat, look to Know Thy Foe: World Eaters, which we just published yesterday for our Warhound readers. 

I am excited to see where the meta goes, with a healthy side eye at Space Marine results. 

New Custodes First Thoughts

Unlike Marines and Orks which had a pretty good consensus on what was going to dominate, Custodes is still looking for a solid path. There are a lot of good datasheets and Detachments, but nothing as crazy as Dakka Rigs or Primarchs to really give theorycrafting a big push in a certain direction. Most top-level players see Custodes as a high B tier or low A tier book, with nothing that is necessarily broken to push it to the top of the meta, but with a lot of exploration to build and play with. Both of these are very good things especially after spending so much time living in either triple Land Raider or 18 Allarus land. We all need a break from Custodes dominating the field. 

The highlights from the book include Trajan, who is the most durable infantry character in the game and possibly the hardest hitting. The Dreadnaughts also look incredible with some great flamer access on incredibly hard hitting melee. The best Detachments seem to focus on increased mobility, with Solar Watch the big winner; turns out giving every unit access to +2 move is pretty good! We've given our initial thoughts on the Codex already, and if you want to dive more into Custodes, look for our beginner guide and Know Thy Foe focusing on them around the corner in just a few weeks. 

Sisters of Silence: Prosecutors - Credit: Pendulin

Player Focus: Sam Pope

If you haven’t been following teams 40k you probably have missed Sam Pope. He isn’t crushing the singles circuit, but he is a monster 40k player. He was part of the winning roster attending WTC in August with Team USA and is a Tyranid faction specialist. That doesn't mean he is stuck in a 'Nids box, however. He brought Chaos Space Marines to WTC for the winning run, and took 70 Khorne Berzerkers to a second place finish at BFS, only losing in the end to John Lennon. While he is not going to end up in ITC contention, landing currently at #759 on the ICT leaderboard and #65 in ELO, he is a force to be reckoned with and someone I am watching going back into teams season. (Sam Pope has his own YouTube channel called “Sam-Pope-40k;” it's very good, go watch it.)

Alongside our coverage of the what's-what of 40k each week, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson joins us to provide some quick updates on the movers and shakers in the competitive scene of some of the other games we cover here at Tabletop Battles!

Khazalite Holds Announced for Preorder

The biggest reveal from the Big Autumn Preview from Games Workshop came in the form of Order’s tiniest defenders, the Khazalite Holds. Unlike their Khardoran cousins, whose steampunk airships are a far cry from what we normally expect out of Dwarves, the warriors of the Khazalite Hold are much more straightforward representations of fantasy Dwarf Archetypes. That’s not to say there isn’t some Age of Sigmar high fantasy flavor, of course: They do have a land boat with a big ol’ throne on it to sail you right towards the nearest bozo in need of clobbering.

With the preorder date set for this upcoming Saturday, we can expect to have our first look at the new army rules and unit profiles over the course of the week on the Warhammer Community website.

A Quieter Weekend for AoS and Kill Team 

After back to back gigantic events with the LGT and LVO, this week is much reduced in tournament activity for Kill Team and Age of Sigmar. That's not to say that there isn’t anything happening though, particularly in the world of Sigmar, where a fairly large team tournament was hosted in Spain. The event, LETANIA DEL OSO II AOS, hosted twenty teams of five battling it out over the course of five rounds. The winner of the event was team Requiem, finishing 4-1 with the highest overall score.

Things will start to pick up again for both game systems later this month, with a few larger 5 round events popping up at the end of October for Kill Team and another huge teams event next weekend for Age of Sigmar, as the format continues to rapidly increase in popularity.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Australia Wins the Warmachine World Team Championship

The biggest event in Warmachine, the World Team Championship (WTC), was held this past weekend in Poland, bringing 240 players from around the world a chance to compete for the chance to bring home the coveted WTC trophy for their home country. The event hosts any country able and willing to send players to compete in teams of at least five, and has changed venues from year to year to celebrate the diverse player base of Warmachine. This year, the winning team was team Charging Cassowaries from Australia, whose team makeup was notable for lacking any player piloting Fane of Nyrro, the current boogeyman of the Warmachine metagame. Second place was won by England’s Team Lancelot, and third was won by USA’s Team Death Valley.

Alongside these winners, the WTC announced the host for next year’s event is Dusseldorf, Germany, and the bidding process will soon open for the 2028 host country.

StarCraft TMG Reveals Wave 3 Alongside Release Roadmap

Archon Studios has been experiencing massive success with StarCraft: The Miniatures Game, and as Wave 2 is starting to hit store shelves and player hands Archon decided to pull the curtain back on what the next wave of the game looks like. 

Alongside a major patch to improve the balance of the races, Archon released the rules cards for the third wave expansion for SC:TMG. Each faction picks up a new hero and support style unit with this release, with the Ghost Nova and the flying Raven joining the Terran, the High Templars and Tassadar reinforcing the Zerg, and Zagara and the Defiler joining the Zerg roster. Preorders for Wave 3 open on October 12th, with an expected street date of early November. 

Alongside these releases, Archon gave us an updated roadmap look for what we can expect in late 2026 and in 2027, with a few very interesting tidbits to see. The most notable of these is the announcement of a new 2 player limited edition starter pack releasing this December, pitting the Zerg led by Infested Stukhov and Infested Terran forces against Alarak and his Tal’Darim Protoss. The release will also include bits to add on to the Terran Siege Tank to run as an Infested Siege Tank, so the Terran can no longer hog all of the fun.

Halo’s Next Expansion is Bringing the Covenant Proper to the Tabletop

It’s a pretty dreadful time to be a Halo fan right now -- unless you’re a fan of the Halo Tabletop Game from Mantic, in which case it is a very exciting time. 

On Friday, Mantic announced its next release of Halo: Judgement, which brings the original bad guys of Halo, the Covenant, properly on to the Tabletop for the first time. The expansion box includes the Prophet of Regret, one of the leaders of the fanatical Covenant cult hellbent on cleansing the universe, alongside  Elite Honor Guard and Rangers and the hulking Hunters. Joining the fight against the Covenant is one of the most iconic characters of the franchise, Sergeant Johnson, one of Master Chief's closest companions from the original trilogy of games and a fan favorite.

Alongside the Judgement expansion, Mantic is releasing the Halo Campaign Evolved board game, designed to be played by 1-2 players and focused on recreating some of the most iconic events from the Halo franchise, such as the escape from the Pillar of Autumn from the very first game. The game comes with standee miniatures for a wide array of covenant forces as well as a plastic Elite Zealot miniature, and a miniature for Master Chief himself to boot. You can’t expect to talk about the biggest moments from Halo without the Master Chief!

Wizards Reveals Next Marvel Crossover Set at New York Comic Con

New York Comic Con, one of the biggest conventions for general geek and pop culture in the world, was held this past weekend, and Wizards of the Coast brought some exciting reveals along to showcase to attendees. One of the most significant of these reveals was the announcement of the next Universes Beyond crossover set, Marvel: Darkhold Destiny. Unlike previous Universes Beyond sets, which focused on homage over storytelling, Darkhold is treading entirely new ground for Universes Beyond by telling its own original story with this set release. With this storytelling focus in mind, Marvel is releasing a tie-in comic introducing a brand new character from Darkhold to go along with the set, which will release digitally before the wider set release in April 2027, written by Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly. 

While it’s unlikely that every Universes Beyond set will be set up like this, it is very exciting to know that Wizards wants to push beyond just using these sets as fan service and are instead trying to push the boundary of collaboration by telling new stories with the unique storytelling stylings that so many players love about Magic.

title: Contemptor Kevin's Las Vegas 2026 Recap (Featuring LVO 2026)
content:
One of the drawbacks to living in the Greater Washington D.C. Metropolitan Area is the summer.  Summers in D.C. are known for rather disgusting humidity, to the point where the United States Congress takes August off because for the majority of the first 200 years of the country the capital was too miserable to be in.   Luckily, America has an answer to the humidity of the capital: the dry desert on the other side of the country!  And in that desert, we have Sin City: Las Vegas Nevada.  While hot and brutally sunny, the casino megaresorts are cool and pleasant.  And gaming companies have noticed!  Which is why I, along with RagnarokAngel and many others, went to the LVO 2026.  

But!  The LVO was not my *only* gaming and hobby event to Vegas in 2026.  The LVO is now in October, and you many have noticed that I was talking about August.  Well, in early August of 2026 I decided to leave a particularly rain-hammered DC to go to Vegas for STLV, the convention formerly known as Star Trek Las Vegas.  There, Wizards of the Coast would be having a presentation with Star Trek Strange New Worlds’ Jess Bush for the upcoming Universes Beyond: Star Trek set.  They also were offering demos of the set.   The convention also featured hobby classes.  By going to Vegas early I would *also* be able to scope out the hotel Alice and I were staying at and getting to enjoy certain aspects of Vegas I would not have time to hit while at LVO.  

Part 1: Contemptor Kevin’s Quantum Subspace Tunnel to STLV

STLV is held in the former home of the LVO, the Rio Casino and Resorts.  The good news is that the hotel has been undergoing extensive renovations since January of 2025.  This means that many better amenities from the Rio still existed.  However, the hotel was sold out for part of the time I would be in Vegas.  I therefore decided to get a jump on the hotel that Alice and I would be staying at for LVO: The Excalibur Casino and Resort.  The Excalibur is next door to where we stayed in 2025, and so the two of us had hit the hotel for food and drink a few times last year.  However, since we would be staying there for almost a week, I wanted to make sure the Excalibur was sufficient for our needs.  

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

Reader, the Excalibur was an excellent hotel to stay in.  It had a relatively low cost, was pretty easy to navigate through, and had a large selection of various restaurants, stores, and other amenities from which to enjoy our stay.  They also had $3 margaritas.  We stayed in the refurbished Resort Tower.  This was very close to the gym and not a bad walk from either the main entrance or the rideshare entrance.  The only downside to the room was an insufficient number of outlets for all the technology I needed to plug in and charge.  

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

This year for STLV, Wizards of the Coast decided to debut the upcoming Universes Beyond: Star Trek set for Magic: The Gathering with a full-court press.  The ticket level that I purchased came with one of the welcome decks - sadly, I got the Black welcome deck.  This was disappointing because none of the actors who featured in the set were at the con so I could not get autographed cards this year.  At the Con, they also had a room dedicated to Magic: The Gathering demonstrations.  So I decided to roll up my sleeves, and do something I hadn’t done in 30 years: Play Magic.

I played against a nice fellow from WOTC named Chris, and I played the blue starter deck, since I like Mr. Spock.  While this game was not particularly complicated (as Magic goes), many of the main concepts from Magic have not changed in thirty years.  My deck shuffling was suboptimal, so I wound up drawing a lot of lands to start off with.  This meant that before my life ran out, I drew some big creatures for defense before making my big push.  I won, with two life left.  Hooray!  

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

One of the last major panels for STLV was a discussion between Gavin Verhey and Jess Bush (the actor who plays Nurse Christine Chapel on Star Trek: Strange New Worlds).  Ms. Bush was told stories about how Ethan Peck (Mr. Spock) got her into playing Magic, and was thus given the opportunity to reveal the card based off of her.  We also got to see Ms. Bush twerk it to the Star Trek: The Next Generation theme.  WOTC also handed out a convention exclusive Captain Kirk card - sadly, I was unable to get mine autographed by William Shatner since I did not get a Shatner autograph ticket.  Mr. Verhey also explained that all the Lower Decks-themed cards in the set were of common or uncommon rarity, because they cannot get promoted.

The other hobby-related activity I did at STLV was to go into the room that used to be LVO’s Hobby Hangout and paint.  Creation has started to pay a fellow named Ed Mueller to go to their conventions and host a painting class slash hobby room.  One can get their pictures taken at a slow photo booth with digital inserts of Star Trek cast members, while there was also a jewelry making station.  The centerpiece was a Bob Ross-style painting class, because Mr. Mueller is a certified Bob Ross painter.  The class I took was on using a stencil to paint a canvas with Star Trek ships.  First, we painted a starscape, then selected a stencil outline of a Star Trek ship.  I selected the USS Enterprise E, as that one is my favorite of the TNG-era Enterprise designs.  My goal was to finish my Enterprise painting over the weekend, and luckily I’ve taken enough miniature painting classes to finish.  I had to dive into the vendor’s hall a couple of time to reference some large models of the Enterprise E to get the pattern right, but ultimately I was happy with the outcome.  

The other stuff I did at the convention was 1) shop and 2) meet and greet various Star Trek actors.  Indeed, I’ve never been able to meet the geniuses behind so many Star Trek characters all at once.  

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

STLV was a very fun convention, and a great way to get my appetite whetted for the Las Vegas Open.  While I did wind up having friends in Vegas at the time, I would not realize that my one Warhammer friend was in town until we met back up at LVO.  LVO was therefore set up as my other big vacation for 2026.

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman. The first model I ever saw and where my road to TTB started.

Part 2: The Continuing Adventures of Kevin and Alice

Credit: Alice "RagnarokAngel" Lirette

Alice and I decided early on to get into Vegas early so that we could spend more time at Area 15.  Last year, we wanted to do the new Interstellar Arc.  However, Interstellar Arc would not open until a week after we left Vegas, so that was put at the top of the list for 2026.  There were a plethora of other activities at Area 15 that we wanted to do (the Museum of Ice Cream, the Escape Game franchise, and various food and drink).  Last time we went to Area 15 the two of us were exhausted, so we made sure to hit this first.  

I got in Tuesday night, and immediately went with Alice and her friend Rey to the Venetian for dinner.  Why go from one end of the strip to another?  Because the Venetian has a food court with a Howlin’ Rays franchise.  Howlin’ Rays is a Pasadena-based hot chicken restaurant with huge and excellent chicken tenders.  I have been to their Pasadena location a couple of times in the past, but the Pasadena experience tends to be: 1) During Pokémon Go Fest Tour (so I want to be out catching Pokémon and doing various Pokémon raids) and 2) Require me to spend an hour or so waiting in line.  While GoFest Tour is in late February, Pasadena is pretty sunny and so it’s warm.  This means to avoid sunburn and the phones overheating, I have to huddle under an umbrella.  By contrast, the Venetian location has no line.  I just went up, ordered my tenders and beer, and enjoyed.  

Wednesday morning, after I finished working out, Alice and I Ubered to a local Whole Foods in order to pick up an order of various items we needed delivered: power strips, Monster Zero, Ramen (for Alice to avoid paying hotel snack prices), and various food containers.  Next to the Whole Foods in Vegas was a very large and comprehensive gaming store called Knight and Day Games.  The staff at Knight and Day games, despite it being a random Wednesday morning at 10:00 am, were quite friendly and enthusiastic.  Alice snagged a Magic booster box, while I picked up some primer and additional Ultramarines upgrades for my army.  We also spied the under-construction paint racks for Warhammer Tone Pro.  

Afterwards, we met up with Rey and hit Area 15.  After lunch, we went through the Interstellar Arc.  This is akin to a VR-based exploration game, where we are learning about an attempt in the far future to colonize another planet in an ecologically sound manner.  Beyond the fact that it was quite lovely, it also had a lot to discover.  I only managed about a 67% completion of all the secrets of the Arc, while Alice was able to get up to the 80s.  Next time, I want to come back and see if I can’t get a higher completion percentage.  

The second experience we did was the Museum of Ice Cream.  This involved us having to come up with what ice cream flavor identified us (I was “Calgar Creamcicle”), learning the secrets of toppings, and then ultimately going to the unlimited ice cream bar.  I was a bit disappointed in the ice cream bar because of a lack of peanut butter flavored ice cream.   We also went down various slides to land in giant plastic sprinkles.  Surprisingly safe!  

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

The third experience we did was Alice and I’s first escape room of the trip: The Escape Game’s Prison Break scenario.  I very much enjoyed this room and the unique mechanics behind it.  We were able to escape with 19 seconds left to spare, because we wound up brute forcing a couple of puzzles we were not supposed to brute force.  Still, the theme was fun and the puzzles ingenious.  While in retrospect I would have gone with a different room (that’s unique to Vegas) versus Prison Break (which I can’t do with my home crew), it was still a fun experience.  

Credit: The gamemaster at the Escape Game Area 15

Afterwards, Alice and Rey wanted to hit up the John Wick experience while I had something of an upset stomach and decided to go back to the room and go to bed early.  After the three weeks leading up to the event, I was tired! 

Part 3: Thursday LVO Day One and Kevin’s Gundam Assemble Adventure

Having gone to bed early, I woke up early and worked out.  After I showered, I dragooned Alice and Rey to the Buffet and then the LVO so we could pick up our badges and swag bags.  Unfortunately, they were not able to get into the John Wick experience the night before.  They decided to skip the initial day of LVO to instead go to John Wick and drink.  I got to see my friend Phil from the 2025 Masterclass, and chat with him for awhile.  We’ve met up at the intervening Adepticons, NoVas, and LVOs, and once again we were both doing masterclasses.  I was in Dan Ozborne’s class and he and Nick were taking Jan Soukup's Oils class.  

This year, I had gone with both the High Roller package and the Masterclass package.  Unlike previous conventions where I was handed a bag brimming with miniatures, the vendor swag portion was available through a series of tickets were could take to various booths.  Phil explained to me that was how other conventions (specifically, DefCon) handled attendee swag.  This way we would be encouraged to travel to different booths instead of just having a bunch of random odds and ends in a bag.  Normally at a gaming convention, the 40K booth tends to be the biggest booth and biggest draw. And this year, GW did have their big event store and a table where folks could spend a few minutes trying out the Tone Pro demo kit.  But as Rob pointed out in his two recaps of the LVO, the belle of the LVO ball was Gundam Assemble.

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

Bandai went all-out for the event, with multiple demo tables, photo opportunities, a mini-golf course, and a “scavenger hunt.”  And I made it my quest to do as much as I could on that initial day.  After quickly securing the starter set, I secured time cards to do both the paint demonstration and the gaming demonstration.  I knew absolutely nothing about the game when I did the demo, and found myself pleasantly surprised at the game flow.  The demo was, for the most part, relatively scripted:  We were told which actions to take, with some of the power ups being random and the dice rolls being random.  I liked the pacing of the game, which means I’m not stuck waiting for awhile for my turn.  In the demo, I did not feel as if I had much agency during my opponent’s turn (no saving dice, for example), but we also only had one use of tactics cards in the demo.  I played the Federation side of the board, which let me use the RX-78 Gundam and crush Char and his Zakus.  At the beginning of LVO the demo tables were packed.  Towards the end of the first day, folks were able to just walk up and play.  

My Masterclass pals Nick and Phil. Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

The Scavenger Hunt had four stations: the Lobby photo booth/Gunplay demo, a station at the far end of the convention center lobby (where you had to play a round of mini-golf), a station just inside the convention hall, and a station at the booth.  Every time you completed one of the scavenger quests, you got a new round of flair to add to your badge.  At the end, you received a raffle ticket to win a Gundam Assemble starter set.  Spoiler alert:  I did not win.  As I already had a starter set, this was not a huge disappointment.  

The most interesting part, for me, was the painting demonstration/opportunity.  While the booth was offering promo versions of the three Federation mechs (Guntank, Guncannon, and Gundam RX-78) in yellow plastic for High Rollers and for following them on Instagram, the painting demo was handing out three Zakus: Char’s Zaku, a Zaku II Linebreaker (IIRC the one with the cannon), and Zaku II Enforcer (the one with the axe).  I got handed a Zaku II Linebreaker.  While I am not the first TTB author to get one of these, or even the first TTB author named Kevin to get one of these, I believe I’m the first author to use the new Mr. Hobby Gundam Assemble Color.  

The models were supplied to us on-sprue, and unfortunately for me this was the one time in 2026 where I was at a wargaming event without my hobby supply bag.  I had left it back in the room!  I used the provided clippers and some emery boards I had in my backpack to try and smooth the surface of the Zaku.  After assembling the model, it was time to paint it.  We had a few of the paints: Gundam Assemble Color NGA-05 Black, NGA-04 Red, NGA-08 Light Green, and NGA-45 Dark Green.  I think we might have also had NGA-43 Steel, but I never wound up using it.  These come in screw-top bottles, and do not have internal mixing balls.

I decided to use NGA Black as the base coat, and I believe I made a terrible mistake.  While the paint was able to stick to the plastic relatively fine, the black was very glossy.  Trying to figure out where shapes on the model began or ended was very challenging in the harsh convention center lighting.  The paint was also extremely slow to dry and painting more than one color onto the model in the limited time I had was a struggle.  I was able to get both NGA Light Green and Dark Green onto the model, but I was not very impressed with those initial results.  The booth was also handing out free bottles of NGA White and NGA Blue if you followed them on YouTube.  While I did not have the change to play with them in Vegas, I did once I got home:

The White has decent coverage.  While it doesn't have the same smooth feel as Pro Acryl's Bold Titanium White, my initial tests have the two compare pretty similarly.  Both are very bright, though I felt the NGA White did not want to be thinned down very much.  Sadly, at the time of writing I did not have the opportunity to directly test this against Warhammer Paint Blackstone Void 5 White.  

Left to Right, Top to Bottom: WH Paint Ulthuan Grey, Gundam Assemble Color NGA-01 White, Underlying Vallejo TMM Sapphire Blue, ProAcryl Bold Titanium White. Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

The Blue came out as a dark blue.  It has very good coverage, and is not as purple as Warhammer Paint Macragge Blue.  It is not as bright as Pro Acryl Ultramarine.  It has some similarities with Warhammer Paint Caledor Sky, except maybe a smidge more purple than that.  I used the paint on my Repulsor Executioner's guns for some of the bracketing as the undercoat/shadow color, before highlighting up with Ultramarine and eventually Bold Titanium White.  I was happy with the result.

From left to right, top to bottom: ProAcryl Ultramarine, Gundam Assemble Color NAG-02 Blue, WH Paint Caledor Sky, WH Paint Macragge Blue. Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

In order to paint my Zaku II model at LVO though, I headed over to the Hobby Haven, took my trusty drybrush (a Citadel Medium Drybrush), and asked the Warhammer Tone Pro demo table if I could dab said drybrush in Hierotek Green 3.  While this color did not give me the same drab green that the Zaku II is famous for, the punchy green of Hierotek Green 3 and 5 served to give me a very bold Zaku, and one I was quite proud of speed-painting. 

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

Afterwards, I met up with John “Can you Roll a Crit” Rees to meet him, collect various other High Roller swag bag giveaways, and chat about Gundam Assemble.  He went off to go play the Assemble Demo, while I decided to head back to the hotel and get dinner.  Alice and Rey had returned from their Area 15 adventure, and followed me down into the Excalibur’s food court for food.  I had a good enough but severely overpriced smashburger and fries, then hit the hay.  Tomorrow my Masterclass with Dan Ozborne would begin, and I would have the opportunity to meet new friends, make new friends, and see even more old friends!

Until next time LVOteers!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.
